sections.title: Why a cell never divides on a whim

board_events.text: Why does a cell divide at all?
A cell does not divide on a whim.
It divides only after it has grown to a sufficient size AND faithfully duplicated its entire genetic instruction set.
So that each of the two daughter cells receives a complete, identical copy.
Cell cycle = the whole sequence of events from the birth of a cell to its division into two daughter cells.

board_events.text: Two grossly unequal parts: a long preparation, a brief division.
Preparation is the rule. Division is the exception.

segments.text: <curious>Let me open with a question that sounds obvious but really is not. Why does a cell divide at all, and what has to be true before it is allowed to?
First thing to fix in your head. A cell does not divide on a whim. Division is never a casual decision. It is the end of a long process, not the start of one.
A cell divides only after two conditions are met. It must have grown to a sufficient size, and it must have faithfully duplicated its entire genetic instruction set.
Why insist on both? Because the whole point is that each of the two daughter cells walks away with a complete, identical copy of the instructions. Copy first, then split. Never the other way round.
So here is our definition, and it is worth stating precisely. The cell cycle is the whole sequence of events from the birth of a cell to its division into two daughter cells.

Picture a large Indian wedding. For weeks beforehand nothing visibly dramatic happens, yet the household is humming — shopping, cooking, stitching, doubling up on every arrangement so that two families can be served. Then comes the wedding day itself. A few intense hours where everything that was prepared is finally distributed, and one household becomes two.

The cell works in exactly this rhythm. It spends the overwhelming majority of its life quietly preparing, growing and copying its contents, and only a brief, theatrical window goes on the actual division.
Anchor this for the entire chapter. Preparation is the rule, division is the exception. Every single stage you are about to learn is either part of the long preparation, or part of the brief split.
<curious>चलिए एक सवाल से शुरू करते हैं जो obvious लगता है, पर है नहीं। एक cell divide करता ही क्यों है, और उससे पहले क्या सच होना ज़रूरी है?
सबसे पहली बात दिमाग़ में बिठा लीजिए। Cell किसी whim पर divide नहीं करता। Division कभी casual decision नहीं होता। ये एक लंबे process का अंत है, शुरुआत नहीं।
Cell सिर्फ़ तभी divide करता है जब दो conditions पूरी हों। उसे sufficient size तक grow करना होगा, और अपना पूरा genetic instruction set faithfully duplicate करना होगा।
दोनों पर insist क्यों? क्योंकि पूरा point यही है कि दोनों daughter cells instructions की एक complete, identical copy लेकर जाएँ। पहले copy, फिर split। कभी उल्टा नहीं।
तो हमारी definition ये रही, और इसे precisely कहना ज़रूरी है। Cell cycle मतलब events का वो पूरा sequence, एक cell के जन्म से लेकर उसके दो daughter cells में divide होने तक।

एक बड़ी Indian wedding सोचिए। हफ़्तों तक बाहर से कुछ dramatic नहीं दिखता, फिर भी घर में हलचल है — shopping, cooking, stitching, हर arrangement double किया जा रहा है ताकि दो families serve हो सकें। फिर आता है wedding day। कुछ intense घंटे, जहाँ जो तैयार किया था वो सब बँट जाता है, और एक घर दो हो जाता है।

Cell बिल्कुल इसी rhythm में चलता है। अपनी ज़िंदगी का overwhelming majority हिस्सा वो quietly preparing में बिताता है — growing, अपने contents copy करते हुए। सिर्फ़ एक brief, theatrical window actual division पर जाती है।
पूरे chapter के लिए इसे anchor बना लीजिए। Preparation rule है, division exception है। आगे आप जो भी stage सीखेंगे, वो या तो लंबी preparation का हिस्सा है, या उस brief split का।

sections.title: Interphase and M phase — two grossly unequal parts

board_events.text: The cycle has two grossly unequal parts
INTERPHASE — the long, preparatory phase. Occupies $\gt 95\%$ of the cycle's duration.
It is sometimes called the 'resting phase' — but that name is misleading.
The cell is anything but resting. It is the busiest the cell ever gets: growing, synthesising proteins, and replicating its DNA.

board_events.text: M PHASE (mitotic phase) — the short, dramatic part. The duplicated material is parcelled out equally.
Human cycle: ~24 h total. Interphase ~23 h. M phase under 1 h.
24 hours is a typical value, NOT a fixed constant. A yeast cell finishes the whole cycle in about 90 minutes.

segments.text: The cell cycle splits into exactly two parts, and the striking thing is how lopsided that split is. Let us name both and size them honestly.
The long, preparatory part is called interphase, and it occupies more than ninety five percent of the cycle's duration. That is not a detail — that is almost the whole of the cell's life.
Now, interphase is sometimes called the resting phase. I want you to be suspicious of that name straight away, because it is misleading in a way that examiners love to exploit.

The cell during interphase is anything but resting. This is the busiest the cell ever gets. It is growing, it is synthesising proteins, and crucially, it is replicating its D N A. Resting refers only to the absence of visible division.

Put numbers on it. In a typical human cell the whole cycle takes about twenty four hours. Of that, interphase occupies roughly twenty three hours, and the M phase takes less than a single hour. The dividing itself is brief; the preparation is long.
The short, dramatic part is the M phase, the mitotic phase. This is the actual division, where everything the cell duplicated during interphase is finally parcelled out equally between two daughters.

So the shape of the answer to any timing question is this. Interphase is the marathon, M phase is the sprint at the finish line. If a question asks which phase is longest, the answer is interphase, every time.

One caution before we move on. That neat twenty four hour figure is a typical value, not a fixed constant. Cycle length varies enormously between cell types and organisms. A yeast cell, for instance, completes its entire cycle in about ninety minutes.
Cell cycle ठीक दो parts में बँटता है, और striking बात ये है कि ये split कितना lopsided है। दोनों को name करते हैं और honestly size करते हैं।
लंबे, preparatory part को interphase कहते हैं, और ये cycle की duration का ninety five percent से भी ज़्यादा occupy करता है। ये कोई detail नहीं है — ये cell की लगभग पूरी ज़िंदगी है।
अब, interphase को कभी-कभी resting phase कहा जाता है। मैं चाहता हूँ आप इस name पर तुरंत suspicious हो जाएँ, क्योंकि ये misleading है — और examiners इसी को exploit करना पसंद करते हैं।

Interphase में cell resting तो बिल्कुल नहीं होता। ये cell का सबसे busy दौर है। वो grow कर रहा है, proteins synthesise कर रहा है, और सबसे अहम — अपना D N A replicate कर रहा है। Resting का मतलब सिर्फ़ इतना है कि visible division नहीं दिख रहा।

इस पर numbers रखिए। एक typical human cell में पूरा cycle लगभग twenty four hours लेता है। उसमें से interphase roughly twenty three hours occupy करता है, और M phase एक घंटे से भी कम। Dividing खुद brief है; preparation लंबी है।
छोटा, dramatic part है M phase, यानी mitotic phase. यही actual division है, जहाँ interphase में जो कुछ duplicate हुआ था वो finally दोनों daughters में equally parcel out होता है।
तो किसी भी timing question का shape यही है। Interphase marathon है, M phase finish line पर sprint है। अगर question पूछे कौन सा phase सबसे लंबा है, जवाब हमेशा interphase है।

आगे बढ़ने से पहले एक caution. वो neat twenty four hour figure एक typical value है, fixed constant नहीं। Cycle length cell types और organisms के बीच enormously vary करती है। जैसे एक yeast cell अपना पूरा cycle लगभग ninety minutes में complete कर लेता है।

sections.title: Mitosis is equational — the engine of growth and repair

board_events.text: Mitosis is an EQUATIONAL division
The parent cell and both daughter cells carry the same number and kind of chromosomes.
A cell with 46 chromosomes produces two cells with 46 chromosomes each.

board_events.text: Nothing is halved. Nothing is reshuffled. It is a faithful copy operation.
This is precisely why mitosis is the engine of GROWTH.
One fertilised egg becomes a trillion-celled human — every cell keeping the identical chromosome count.
And of REPAIR: a cut finger heals, a lizard regrows its tail. Mitosis supplies the new cells.

segments.text: Let us characterise mitosis in one word, and that word is equational. Almost everything about how mitosis behaves in an exam question follows from this single property.
Equational means the parent cell and both daughter cells carry the same number, and the same kind, of chromosomes. Note that it is two claims, not one — number and kind.
Concretely, a cell with forty six chromosomes produces two cells with forty six chromosomes each. Not twenty three. Not ninety two. Forty six, and forty six.

The figure makes the shape of it plain. One parent goes in, two daughters come out, and the count on every label is the same. This is the picture to hold when a numerical asks you what the daughters inherit.
So nothing is halved and nothing is reshuffled. Mitosis is a faithful copy operation. Hold on to those two negatives, because meiosis will do exactly both of the things mitosis refuses to do.
This is precisely why mitosis is the engine of growth. Growth needs more cells, but it must not change what those cells are — and equational division delivers exactly that combination.

Sit with the scale of that for a second. A single fertilised egg becomes a trillion celled human, and every one of those trillion cells keeps the identical chromosome count. The copy is repeated a trillion times without drift.

And the same property makes mitosis the engine of repair. When you cut your finger, or a lizard regrows its tail, mitosis supplies the new cells — and they have to be the same cells, which is exactly what equational guarantees.
Mitosis को एक word में characterise करते हैं, और वो word है equational. Exam question में mitosis जैसा भी behave करे, लगभग सब कुछ इसी एक property से निकलता है।
Equational का मतलब है parent cell और दोनों daughter cells same number, और same kind, के chromosomes रखते हैं। ग़ौर कीजिए ये दो दावे हैं, एक नहीं — number और kind.
Concretely, forty six chromosomes वाला cell दो cells बनाता है, हर एक में forty six chromosomes. ना twenty three, ना ninety two. Forty six, और forty six.
Figure इसका shape साफ़ कर देता है। एक parent अंदर जाता है, दो daughters बाहर आती हैं, और हर label पर count वही है। जब कोई numerical पूछे कि daughters को क्या मिला, यही तस्वीर पकड़िए।
तो कुछ half नहीं होता और कुछ reshuffle नहीं होता। Mitosis एक faithful copy operation है। इन दोनों negatives को पकड़े रहिए, क्योंकि meiosis ठीक वही दोनों काम करेगा जिनसे mitosis इनकार करता है।
यही वजह है कि mitosis growth का engine है। Growth को और cells चाहिए, पर वो cells क्या हैं ये बदलना नहीं चाहिए — और equational division ठीक यही combination देता है।
एक पल इस scale के साथ बैठिए। एक fertilised egg trillion celled human बन जाता है, और उन trillion cells में से हर एक identical chromosome count रखता है। Copy एक trillion बार दोहराई जाती है, बिना खिसके।

और यही property mitosis को repair का engine बनाती है। जब आप उंगली काट लेते हैं, या कोई lizard अपनी tail वापस उगाती है, नए cells mitosis ही supply करता है — और उन्हें वही cells होना है, जिसकी guarantee equational देता है।

board_events.text: Caveat 1: mitosis occurs in BOTH haploid and diploid cells — it does not require pairs of chromosomes.
Most mitotic divisions in the body are of diploid somatic cells — but haploid cells divide mitotically too.
The male honeybee (drone) develops from an unfertilised egg and is haploid — yet its cells divide by mitosis.
Meiosis, by contrast, occurs ONLY in diploid cells.
Caveat 2: the 'equational' guarantee holds only when karyokinesis is followed by cytokinesis.
Caveat 3: ~24 hours is a TYPICAL value, never a fixed constant.

segments.text: Equational comes with fine print, and NEET lives in the fine print. There are three assumptions students routinely over-trust here. Let us disarm all three now.
Three panels, three over-trusted assumptions. Read the bold verdict under each one before I explain it — no, usually, no.

Caveat one. Mitosis occurs in both haploid and diploid cells. It does not require pairs of chromosomes at all. Nothing in prophase, metaphase, anaphase or telophase asks a chromosome to find a partner.

Most mitotic divisions in the body are of diploid somatic cells, which is why the diploid case feels like the rule. But haploid cells divide mitotically too — in some lower plants, and in some social insects.

The example to quote is the male honeybee, the drone. It develops from an unfertilised egg, so it is haploid, and yet its cells divide by mitosis perfectly happily. One named example is enough to settle any assertion about this.

Hold that against meiosis, which we meet in the next part. Meiosis occurs only in diploid cells. So if a question says a haploid cell is dividing, mitosis is possible and meiosis is not. That asymmetry is worth a mark on its own.

Caveat two. The equational guarantee holds only when nuclear division is actually followed by cytoplasmic division. In some organisms the nucleus divides but the cytoplasm does not, producing a multinucleate cell. So one division equals two cells is a usual case, not a law.

And caveat three, which we have already met. The neat twenty four hour timing is a typical value, never a fixed constant. Treat every number in this chapter as a representative figure unless the question hands it to you directly.
Equational के साथ fine print आता है, और N E E T उसी fine print में रहता है। यहाँ तीन assumptions हैं जिन पर students routinely ज़रूरत से ज़्यादा भरोसा कर लेते हैं। तीनों को अभी disarm कर लेते हैं।
तीन panels, तीन over-trusted assumptions. हर एक के नीचे bold verdict पढ़िए, उससे पहले कि मैं समझाऊँ — no, usually, no.

Caveat one. Mitosis haploid और diploid, दोनों cells में होता है। उसे chromosomes के pairs की ज़रूरत ही नहीं। Prophase, metaphase, anaphase या telophase में कुछ भी किसी chromosome से partner ढूँढने को नहीं कहता।

Body में ज़्यादातर mitotic divisions diploid somatic cells के होते हैं, इसीलिए diploid case rule जैसा लगता है। पर haploid cells भी mitotically divide करते हैं — कुछ lower plants में, और कुछ social insects में।

Quote करने लायक़ example है male honeybee, यानी drone. वो unfertilised egg से develop होता है, तो haploid है, और फिर भी उसके cells आराम से mitosis से divide करते हैं। इस बारे में किसी भी assertion को निपटाने के लिए एक named example काफ़ी है।

इसे meiosis के सामने रखिए, जो हम अगले part में मिलेंगे। Meiosis सिर्फ़ diploid cells में होता है। तो अगर question कहे कि एक haploid cell divide कर रहा है, mitosis possible है और meiosis नहीं। ये asymmetry अकेले एक mark की है।

Caveat two. Equational guarantee तभी टिकती है जब nuclear division के बाद सचमुच cytoplasmic division हो। कुछ organisms में nucleus divide होता है पर cytoplasm नहीं, और multinucleate cell बन जाता है। तो एक division बराबर दो cells — ये usual case है, law नहीं।

और caveat three, जो हम मिल चुके हैं। वो neat twenty four hour timing एक typical value है, कभी fixed constant नहीं। इस chapter के हर number को representative figure मानिए, जब तक question ख़ुद आपको वो number ना दे।

board_events.text: Interphase has three sub-phases
G1 (Gap 1): the interval between the previous mitosis and the start of DNA synthesis.
The cell is metabolically active and grows, but DNA is NOT yet replicated. Each chromosome has a single chromatid.
Why a gap before copying? Because replication is metabolically expensive and irreversible.

board_events.text: S (Synthesis): DNA replication occurs. Histone protein synthesis accompanies it. In animal cells, the centriole also duplicates.
G2 (Gap 2): proteins are synthesised and the cell grows further, in preparation for mitosis. Replication is complete.
By the end of G2, the cell is poised — licensed — to enter mitosis.

segments.text: Interphase is more than ninety five percent of the cycle, so we cannot leave it as one undifferentiated block. It is subdivided into three sub phases, and each one has a distinct job.
First, G one, or Gap one. This is the interval between the previous mitosis and the start of D N A synthesis. A freshly born cell arrives here and takes stock of its surroundings and its own size.

In G one the cell is metabolically active and it grows, but the D N A is not yet replicated. Chromosome number is the parental number, and each chromosome consists of a single chromatid. Remember that last detail — we will contrast it in a moment.

Why does the cell bother with a gap before copying at all? Because replication is metabolically expensive and it is irreversible. Committing to it without enough resources, or without the right signals, would be wasteful. G one is where that decision gets made.

Look at the two rows underneath the three boxes, because those two rows are the whole examination story. The D N A row changes as you cross S. The chromosome row does not change anywhere in interphase.

Second, S phase, for synthesis. This is where D N A replication actually occurs. Two things ride along with it that students forget. Histone protein synthesis accompanies replication, and in animal cells the centriole also duplicates during this phase.

Third, G two, or Gap two. Here proteins are synthesised — including the spindle components the cell will shortly need — and the cell continues to grow. Replication is already complete by the time G two begins.
By the end of G two the cell is poised, and I would say licensed, to enter mitosis. Everything it needs is built, everything it owns is copied. Only the sorting remains.
Interphase cycle का ninety five percent से ज़्यादा है, तो इसे एक undifferentiated block नहीं छोड़ सकते। ये तीन sub phases में subdivide होता है, और हर एक का अलग काम है।
पहला, G one, यानी Gap one. ये previous mitosis और D N A synthesis की शुरुआत के बीच का interval है। एक freshly born cell यहाँ आता है और अपने surroundings और अपने size का जायज़ा लेता है।

G one में cell metabolically active है और grow करता है, पर D N A अभी replicate नहीं हुआ। Chromosome number parental number है, और हर chromosome में single chromatid है। ये आख़िरी detail याद रखिए — थोड़ी देर में हम इसे contrast करेंगे।

पर cell copying से पहले एक gap क्यों रखता है? क्योंकि replication metabolically expensive है और irreversible है। बिना enough resources के, या बिना सही signals के उसमें commit करना wasteful होगा। वो decision G one में ही लिया जाता है।
तीन boxes के नीचे वाली दो rows देखिए, क्योंकि examination की पूरी कहानी उन्हीं दो rows में है। D N A row S पार करते ही बदलती है। Chromosome row interphase में कहीं भी नहीं बदलती।

दूसरा, S phase, यानी synthesis. यहीं D N A replication असल में होता है। दो चीज़ें इसके साथ चलती हैं जो students भूल जाते हैं। Histone protein synthesis replication के साथ होता है, और animal cells में centriole भी इसी phase में duplicate होता है।

तीसरा, G two, यानी Gap two. यहाँ proteins synthesise होते हैं — spindle components भी, जिनकी ज़रूरत cell को अभी पड़ने वाली है — और cell grow करता रहता है। G two शुरू होने तक replication already complete हो चुका होता है।
G two के अंत तक cell poised होता है — मैं कहूँगा licensed — mitosis में जाने के लिए। जो चाहिए वो बन चुका, जो उसका है वो copy हो चुका। सिर्फ़ sorting बाक़ी है।

board_events.text: The AMOUNT of DNA per cell doubles: $2C \to 4C$.
The NUMBER of chromosomes does NOT change.
A chromosome that was one chromatid is now two sister chromatids held together at the centromere — still counted as ONE chromosome.
This is the source of the single most common exam trap in the whole chapter.
Track DNA amount and chromosome number in two SEPARATE columns.
Also in S phase: histone proteins are synthesised; in animal cells the centriole duplicates.

segments.text: <excited>This section is the single highest yield minute in the whole chapter. If you take away one idea today, take away this one.

Look at the figure before I say anything. On the left, before S phase, one chromosome made of one chromatid. On the right, after S phase, that same chromosome now made of two identical sister chromatids joined at a single centromere. Count the centromeres, not the rods.
Here is what changes. The amount of D N A per cell doubles. If the cell held two C worth of D N A going in, it holds four C coming out. That part everybody gets right.
And here is what does not change. The number of chromosomes. Not one new chromosome is created in S phase. The count going in equals the count coming out.

So how do we reconcile those? Like this. A chromosome that was one chromatid is now two sister chromatids, held together at the centromere. Because they share one centromere, they are still counted as one chromosome. Two chromatids, one chromosome.

This is the source of the single most common exam trap in the whole chapter. A question will double the D N A and then ask for the chromosome number, hoping you will double that too. Do not take the bait.

The defence is mechanical, and I want you to make it a habit. Whenever a numerical gives you both quantities, track D N A amount and chromosome number in two separate columns. Never let one drag the other along.

Two supporting facts to file alongside. Histone protein synthesis accompanies replication, and in animal cells the centriole duplicates during S phase. C U E T in particular likes asking where the centriole doubles.
<excited>ये section पूरे chapter का सबसे highest yield minute है। अगर आज आप एक ही idea लेकर जाएँ, तो यही लेकर जाइए।

मेरे कुछ कहने से पहले figure देखिए। बाईं तरफ़, S phase से पहले, एक chromosome जो एक chromatid से बना है। दाईं तरफ़, S phase के बाद, वही chromosome अब दो identical sister chromatids से बना है, एक single centromere पर जुड़े हुए। Rods मत गिनिए, centromeres गिनिए।
जो बदलता है वो ये है। Cell में D N A की amount double हो जाती है। अगर जाते वक़्त cell में two C worth D N A था, तो निकलते वक़्त four C है। ये हिस्सा सब सही कर लेते हैं।
और जो नहीं बदलता वो ये है। Chromosomes की संख्या। S phase में एक भी नया chromosome नहीं बनता। जाते वक़्त की count निकलते वक़्त की count के बराबर है।

तो इन दोनों को reconcile कैसे करें? ऐसे। जो chromosome एक chromatid था वो अब दो sister chromatids है, centromere पर एक साथ जुड़े हुए। क्योंकि वो एक centromere share करते हैं, उन्हें अब भी एक chromosome गिना जाता है। दो chromatids, एक chromosome.
यही पूरे chapter के सबसे common exam trap की जड़ है। Question D N A double करेगा और फिर chromosome number पूछेगा, इस उम्मीद में कि आप उसे भी double कर देंगे। इस चारे में मत फँसिए।
बचाव mechanical है, और मैं चाहता हूँ आप इसे आदत बना लें। जब भी कोई numerical दोनों quantities दे, D N A amount और chromosome number को दो अलग columns में track कीजिए। एक को दूसरे को खींचने मत दीजिए।

साथ में दो supporting facts file कर लीजिए। Histone protein synthesis replication के साथ चलता है, और animal cells में centriole S phase में duplicate होता है। ख़ासकर C U E T पूछना पसंद करता है कि centriole कहाँ double होता है।

board_events.text: They remain metabolically active but stop proliferating.
They often undergo differentiation into specialised cell types.
Examples of cells sitting in G0: nerve cells and muscle cells.
G0 cells may re-enter the cycle if signalled.
G0 is OUT of the cycle — it is not a fourth gap phase within it.

segments.text: Not every cell that finishes a division goes round again. Some step off the ride entirely, and the place they step off into has a name — G zero.
Cells that will not divide further exit the cycle from G one, and enter G zero. Note the exit point carefully. They leave from G one — never from S, never from G two.
Look at where G zero sits in the figure. It is off to the side, outside the ring. That geometry is the answer to a very common conceptual question, and I will make it explicit in a moment.
What are those cells doing in G zero? They remain metabolically active. This is not death and it is not dormancy in any sloppy sense — the cell is working. What it has stopped doing is proliferating.

In fact G zero is where a lot of the interesting biology happens. Cells there often undergo differentiation into specialised cell types. Stopping division is frequently the price of becoming something specific.
The standard examples you should be able to name are nerve cells and muscle cells. These sit in G zero, which is exactly why nerve and muscle damage heals so poorly compared with, say, skin.
One important qualifier. G zero is not always a one way door. Cells there may re enter the cycle if they are signalled to. So describe G zero as quiescent, not as permanent.

And the point that figure was making. G zero is out of the cycle, not a station within it. It is not a fourth gap phase sitting after G two. Students who list G one, S, G two and G zero as the four sub phases of interphase are getting this wrong.
हर cell जो division ख़त्म करता है, दोबारा चक्कर नहीं लगाता। कुछ ride से पूरी तरह उतर जाते हैं, और जहाँ वो उतरते हैं उसका नाम है G zero.
जो cells आगे divide नहीं करेंगे, वो G one से cycle छोड़ते हैं और G zero में चले जाते हैं। Exit point ध्यान से नोट कीजिए। वो G one से निकलते हैं — कभी S से नहीं, कभी G two से नहीं।
Figure में देखिए G zero कहाँ बैठा है। वो एक तरफ़ है, ring के बाहर. यही geometry एक बहुत common conceptual question का जवाब है, और मैं इसे थोड़ी देर में explicit कर दूँगा।
वो cells G zero में कर क्या रहे हैं? वो metabolically active रहते हैं। ये ना मौत है, ना किसी sloppy sense में dormancy — cell काम कर रहा है। उसने सिर्फ़ proliferate करना बंद किया है।
दरअसल बहुत सारी interesting biology G zero में ही होती है। वहाँ cells अक्सर differentiation से गुज़रकर specialised cell types बन जाते हैं। कुछ specific बनने की क़ीमत अक्सर division छोड़ना ही होती है।
Standard examples जो आपको name करने आने चाहिए — nerve cells और muscle cells. ये G zero में बैठे रहते हैं, और इसीलिए nerve और muscle damage skin के मुक़ाबले इतनी ख़राब तरह से heal होता है।
एक ज़रूरी qualifier. G zero हमेशा one way door नहीं है। वहाँ के cells signal मिलने पर cycle में दोबारा enter कर सकते हैं। तो G zero को quiescent कहिए, permanent नहीं।

और वो point जो figure बना रहा था। G zero cycle के बाहर है, उसके अंदर का station नहीं। ये G two के बाद बैठा कोई fourth gap phase नहीं है। जो students G one, S, G two और G zero को interphase के चार sub phases की तरह list करते हैं, वो ग़लत कर रहे हैं।

board_events.text: Library analogy: photocopy every book BEFORE sorting the collections into two rooms.
Begin sorting before copying is finished, and one branch ends up missing books — a catastrophe.
Progression is driven by regulatory proteins called CYCLINS, acting together with CYCLIN-DEPENDENT KINASES (CDKs).
In scope: the named G1/S and G2/M check points, and the cyclin-CDK mechanism.
Beyond scope: specific cyclin-CDK complexes, the restriction point R, and p53 / Rb.

segments.text: We have said twice now that the cell only divides once conditions are met. Who actually checks? The answer is a system of check points, and it is worth a section of its own.
The cycle is controlled at check points, principally at two transitions — G one to S, and G two to M. Learn those two by name, because that is exactly how they are asked.
See the two red gates in the figure, one before S and one before M. Those are the quality control stations. Each one verifies that a stage is complete before allowing the next to begin.

Here is the intuition. Imagine a library that must split into two identical branches. It must photocopy every single book first — that is replication in interphase. Only then can the staff start sorting the two complete collections into two rooms.

And if they began sorting before the copying finished? One branch ends up missing books. For a library that is annoying; for a cell it is a catastrophe, because a daughter cell missing genes may not survive at all.

Now the machinery. Progression through those gates is driven by regulatory proteins called cyclins, acting together with cyclin dependent kinases, abbreviated C D Ks. Cyclins are the signal, C D Ks are the executor — neither works alone.
Be clear about how deep to go. The named G one to S and G two to M check points, plus the cyclin and C D K mechanism, are within your scope and worth knowing properly.

What is beyond your syllabus at this level — the deeper molecular control, specific cyclin C D K complexes, the restriction point R, and tumour suppressor proteins like p fifty three and R b. Recognise the names if you meet them, but do not spend revision time there.
हम दो बार कह चुके हैं कि cell तभी divide करता है जब conditions पूरी हों। पर असल में check कौन करता है? जवाब है check points का एक system, और ये अपने एक section का हक़दार है।
Cycle check points पर control होता है, मुख्यतः दो transitions पर — G one to S, और G two to M. इन दोनों को name से याद कीजिए, क्योंकि इन्हें बिल्कुल इसी तरह पूछा जाता है।
Figure में दो red gates देखिए, एक S से पहले और एक M से पहले। यही quality control stations हैं। हर एक verify करता है कि कोई stage complete है, तभी अगले को शुरू होने देता है।

Intuition ये रही। एक library सोचिए जिसे दो identical branches में बँटना है। उसे पहले हर एक किताब photocopy करनी होगी — यही interphase में replication है। तभी staff दोनों complete collections को दो कमरों में sort करना शुरू कर सकता है।

और अगर copying ख़त्म होने से पहले sorting शुरू कर दें? एक branch में किताबें कम रह जाएँगी। Library के लिए ये annoying है; cell के लिए catastrophe है, क्योंकि जिस daughter cell में genes कम हों वो शायद survive ही ना करे।

अब machinery. उन gates से progression regulatory proteins से चलता है जिन्हें cyclins कहते हैं, जो cyclin dependent kinases के साथ मिलकर काम करते हैं — short में C D Ks. Cyclins signal हैं, C D Ks executor हैं — कोई अकेले काम नहीं करता।
कितनी गहराई तक जाना है ये साफ़ रखिए। Named G one to S और G two to M check points, plus cyclin और C D K mechanism — ये आपके scope में हैं और ठीक से जानने लायक़ हैं।

इस level पर आपके syllabus से बाहर क्या है — deeper molecular control, specific cyclin C D K complexes, restriction point R, और tumour suppressor proteins जैसे p fifty three और R b. मिलें तो नाम पहचान लीजिए, पर वहाँ revision time मत लगाइए।

board_events.text: Karyokinesis = division of the nucleus. Cytokinesis = division of the cytoplasm.
Mitosis = the four stages of karyokinesis: Prophase $\to$ Metaphase $\to$ Anaphase $\to$ Telophase.
Memory aid: PMAT — 'Please Make A Two'.
Karyokinesis and cytokinesis can come apart — and when they do, you get a syncytium.

segments.text: We now cross into the M phase, the short and dramatic part. Before we walk the stages, let us get the architecture right, because M phase is not one event — it is two.
M phase is the shortest period of the whole cycle — under an hour in a human cell against roughly twenty three hours of interphase — and yet it is the most dramatic.

And here is why it earns all the textbook attention. It is the only stage in which chromosome movements are visible under the microscope. Everything else is invisible bookkeeping; this is the part you can actually watch.
The figure gives you the architecture. M phase comprises karyokinesis, the division of the nucleus, and then cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm. Two separate operations, in that order.

Say those two definitions back to yourself until they are automatic. Karyokinesis is division of the nucleus. Cytokinesis is division of the cytoplasm. They are not synonyms, and treating them as one word is a real source of lost marks.

And note precisely what the word mitosis refers to. Mitosis is the four stages of karyokinesis — prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Cytokinesis follows mitosis; strictly, it is not one of mitosis's stages.
Lock the order with the mnemonic P M A T — please make a two. Which is a nice fit, because making two is precisely what the whole exercise is for.

Keep one loose thread in mind, because we will pull it later. Karyokinesis and cytokinesis can come apart. When the nucleus divides and the cytoplasm does not, you do not get two cells — you get one cell with many nuclei.
अब हम M phase में घुसते हैं, वो छोटा और dramatic हिस्सा। Stages चलने से पहले architecture ठीक कर लेते हैं, क्योंकि M phase एक event नहीं है — दो हैं।
M phase पूरे cycle का सबसे छोटा period है — human cell में एक घंटे से कम, जबकि interphase roughly twenty three hours — और फिर भी सबसे dramatic।

और इसे सारा textbook attention क्यों मिलता है, वजह ये है। ये अकेला stage है जिसमें chromosome movements microscope के नीचे दिखते हैं। बाक़ी सब invisible bookkeeping है; ये वो हिस्सा है जो आप सचमुच देख सकते हैं।
Figure आपको architecture दे रहा है। M phase में आता है karyokinesis, यानी nucleus का division, और फिर cytokinesis, यानी cytoplasm का division. दो अलग operations, इसी order में।

इन दोनों definitions को अपने आप को तब तक दोहराइए जब तक automatic ना हो जाएँ। Karyokinesis मतलब nucleus का division. Cytokinesis मतलब cytoplasm का division. ये synonyms नहीं हैं, और इन्हें एक शब्द मान लेना सचमुच marks गँवाता है।

और ग़ौर कीजिए कि mitosis शब्द किसकी तरफ़ इशारा करता है। Mitosis यानी karyokinesis के चार stages — prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Cytokinesis mitosis के बाद आता है; strictly, वो mitosis का stage नहीं है।
Order को mnemonic से lock कीजिए — P M A T, यानी please make a two. ये fit भी अच्छा बैठता है, क्योंकि दो बनाना ही तो पूरी कवायद का मक़सद है।

एक loose thread दिमाग़ में रखिए, क्योंकि हम इसे बाद में खींचेंगे। Karyokinesis और cytokinesis अलग हो सकते हैं। जब nucleus divide हो और cytoplasm ना हो, तो आपको दो cells नहीं मिलते — एक cell मिलता है कई nuclei वाला।

board_events.text: Centromere — the constriction where the two sister chromatids are held together.
Kinetochore — the specialised protein structure AT the centromere, to which spindle microtubules attach.
Equatorial / metaphase plate — the plane at the cell's equator where chromosomes align in metaphase.
Karyokinesis — nuclear division. Cytokinesis — cytoplasmic division: cleavage furrow in animal cells, cell plate in plant cells.
Syncytium — a multinucleate cell formed when karyokinesis is NOT followed by cytokinesis.
Classic example of a syncytium: the liquid endosperm of a coconut.

segments.text: Before we walk P M A T stage by stage, we need the vocabulary. Every one of these words shows up in the stage descriptions, and half the exam traps in this chapter are really vocabulary traps.
Study the labels on this figure. Centromere, kinetochore, spindle fibre, equatorial plate. Four names, four distinct structures — and the first two are the ones students most often merge into one.

Start with the centromere. It is the constriction at which the two sister chromatids are held together. It is a region of the chromosome itself. That is the structure whose splitting we will make a fuss about in anaphase.

Now the kinetochore. It is the specialised protein structure at the centromere, and it is the thing to which spindle microtubules actually attach. So the relationship is this — the kinetochore sits on the centromere. Same location, different structure, different job.

Third, the equatorial plate, also called the metaphase plate. Careful here — it is not a physical plate of material. It is a plane at the cell's equator, the imaginary line along which the chromosomes align during metaphase.

Our two division words again, now with their mechanisms attached. Karyokinesis is nuclear division. Cytokinesis is cytoplasmic division, achieved by a cleavage furrow in animal cells and by a cell plate in plant cells.

And now the loose thread from last section gets its name. A syncytium is a multinucleate cell, formed when karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis. The nucleus divided, again and again; the cytoplasm never did.

The classic example, and the one that shows up in questions, is the liquid endosperm of a coconut. Coconut water is a syncytium. Remember it as a picture and you will never have to recall the definition cold.
P M A T को stage by stage चलने से पहले हमें vocabulary चाहिए। इनमें से हर शब्द stage descriptions में आता है, और इस chapter के आधे exam traps असल में vocabulary traps ही हैं।
इस figure के labels ध्यान से देखिए। Centromere, kinetochore, spindle fibre, equatorial plate. चार नाम, चार अलग structures — और पहले दो को students सबसे ज़्यादा एक में मिला देते हैं।
Centromere से शुरू करते हैं। ये वो constriction है जहाँ दोनों sister chromatids एक साथ पकड़े हुए हैं। ये chromosome का अपना एक region है। इसी structure के splitting का हम anaphase में शोर मचाएँगे।

अब kinetochore. ये centromere पर बैठा specialised protein structure है, और spindle microtubules असल में इसी से attach होते हैं। तो रिश्ता ये है — kinetochore centromere पर बैठता है। जगह वही, structure अलग, काम अलग।

तीसरा, equatorial plate, जिसे metaphase plate भी कहते हैं। यहाँ सावधान — ये material की कोई physical plate नहीं है। ये cell के equator पर एक plane है, वो imaginary line जिसके साथ metaphase में chromosomes align होते हैं।

हमारे दो division words फिर से, अब mechanisms के साथ। Karyokinesis यानी nuclear division. Cytokinesis यानी cytoplasmic division, जो animal cells में cleavage furrow से और plant cells में cell plate से होता है।
और अब पिछले section का loose thread अपना नाम पा लेता है। Syncytium एक multinucleate cell है, जो तब बनता है जब karyokinesis के बाद cytokinesis ना हो। Nucleus बार-बार divide हुआ; cytoplasm कभी नहीं।
Classic example, और वही जो questions में आता है — coconut का liquid endosperm. नारियल पानी एक syncytium है। इसे तस्वीर की तरह याद रखिए, फिर definition कभी ठंडे दिमाग़ से याद नहीं करनी पड़ेगी।

board_events.text: The diffuse chromatin condenses into compact, visible chromosomes.
You cannot sort threads that are tangled — so the cell coils them tightly first.
Each chromosome appears as TWO sister chromatids — the S-phase duplication is now visible.
The centrosomes (with their centrioles in animal cells) migrate toward opposite poles and begin organising the mitotic spindle.
By the END of prophase: the nucleolus, Golgi complex, endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear envelope are no longer visible.
The envelope must break down so the spindle can REACH the chromosomes. Envelope gone by END of PROPHASE — not metaphase.

segments.text: Prophase opens mitosis, and it has two jobs running in parallel. Tidy the genetic material, and build the machine that will move it.
Follow the figure from left to right. Early prophase — the envelope is still there and the chromatin is condensing. Late prophase — the envelope is gone and the spindle is organising from the poles.
Job one. The diffuse chromatin condenses into compact, visible chromosomes. This is the first moment in the entire cycle at which you can actually see individual chromosomes.

Why condense at all? Because you cannot sort threads that are tangled. Try separating a heap of loose wool into two equal heaps and you will fail; wind it into balls first and it becomes trivial. The cell coils its chromatin tightly for exactly that reason.

And now the S phase work becomes visible. Each chromosome appears as two sister chromatids. Nothing new happened here — those chromatids were made back in S phase. Prophase just makes them possible to see.

Job two, running alongside. The centrosomes, carrying their centrioles in animal cells, migrate toward opposite poles and begin organising the mitotic spindle. Remember the centriole duplicated back in S phase — this is what it duplicated for.

By the end of prophase, a whole list of structures has disappeared. The nucleolus, the Golgi complex, the endoplasmic reticulum, and the nuclear envelope are all no longer visible. Learn that as a list — Boards ask for it directly.

And the reason the envelope in particular must go — the spindle is outside the nucleus, the chromosomes are inside it. The envelope must break down so the spindle can reach them. File this with care, because writing metaphase instead of prophase for envelope breakdown loses marks every single year.
Prophase mitosis को खोलता है, और इसके दो काम साथ-साथ चलते हैं। Genetic material को तैयार करना, और वो machine बनाना जो उसे हिलाएगी।
Figure को बाएँ से दाएँ follow कीजिए। Early prophase — envelope अब भी है और chromatin condense हो रहा है। Late prophase — envelope जा चुका और spindle poles से organise हो रहा है।
पहला काम. Diffuse chromatin condense होकर compact, visible chromosomes बन जाता है। पूरे cycle में यही पहला moment है जब आप individual chromosomes सचमुच देख सकते हैं।

Condense करना ही क्यों है? क्योंकि उलझे हुए threads को sort नहीं किया जा सकता। ढीली ऊन के ढेर को दो बराबर ढेरों में बाँटकर देखिए, नहीं होगा; पहले गोले बना लीजिए, फिर आसान है। Cell अपना chromatin ठीक इसी वजह से कसकर coil करता है।
और अब S phase का काम दिखने लगता है। हर chromosome दो sister chromatids की तरह दिखता है। यहाँ कुछ नया नहीं हुआ — वो chromatids S phase में ही बने थे। Prophase बस उन्हें दिखने लायक़ बनाता है।

दूसरा काम, साथ-साथ चलता हुआ। Centrosomes, animal cells में अपने centrioles के साथ, opposite poles की तरफ़ migrate करते हैं और mitotic spindle organise करना शुरू करते हैं। याद कीजिए centriole S phase में duplicate हुआ था — इसी के लिए हुआ था।

Prophase के अंत तक structures की एक पूरी list ग़ायब हो जाती है। Nucleolus, Golgi complex, endoplasmic reticulum, और nuclear envelope — कोई नहीं दिखता। इसे list की तरह याद कीजिए — Boards इसे सीधे पूछते हैं।

और envelope को ख़ासतौर पर क्यों जाना है — spindle nucleus के बाहर है, chromosomes अंदर। Envelope को टूटना ही होगा ताकि spindle उन तक पहुँच सके। इसे संभालकर file कीजिए, क्योंकि envelope breakdown के लिए prophase की जगह metaphase लिखना हर साल marks गँवाता है।

board_events.text: With the nuclear envelope fully gone, spindle fibres attach to the KINETOCHORES at each chromosome's centromere.
They manoeuvre all the chromosomes to lie at the cell's equator, forming the METAPHASE (equatorial) PLATE.
Why line them up? So that when separation occurs, each pole receives exactly ONE chromatid from EVERY chromosome.
Chromosomes are most condensed and least overlapping at metaphase.
This is why metaphase is the BEST stage for studying chromosome morphology and number (karyotyping).
Interphase is longer, but its chromatin is decondensed and diffuse — chromosomes cannot be resolved.

segments.text: Metaphase is the stage of arrangement. Nothing separates here, nothing condenses further in any dramatic way — this is the cell lining up its cargo before the move.
Look at the arrangement in the figure. Every chromosome, each still made of two chromatids, sits on one central plane. Spindle fibres run from both poles to the kinetochores.

Here is the sequence. With the nuclear envelope now fully gone, spindle fibres can reach in and attach to the kinetochores at each chromosome's centromere. Note the precision of that sentence — fibres attach to kinetochores, not to centromeres, and not to chromosome arms.

The fibres then manoeuvre all the chromosomes until they lie at the cell's equator. That plane is the metaphase plate, also called the equatorial plate. Both names are acceptable and both appear in question papers.

Why go to all this trouble to line them up? Because of what happens next. If every chromosome sits on the midline with its two chromatids facing opposite poles, then when separation occurs each pole receives exactly one chromatid from every chromosome. The alignment is what makes the split fair.
Now a second, quite different property of this stage. At metaphase the chromosomes are the most condensed they ever get, and because they are spread on a single plane, they are the least overlapping.

And that is precisely why metaphase is the best stage for studying chromosome morphology and number. Karyotyping is done on metaphase cells for exactly this reason — maximally condensed, individually distinguishable.

<curious>But hold on, interphase is far longer — why not study chromosomes there? Because length is not the criterion, resolvability is. In interphase the chromatin is decondensed and diffuse, so individual chromosomes simply cannot be resolved. Longest and most suitable are two different questions, and NEET pairs them deliberately.
Metaphase arrangement का stage है। यहाँ कुछ separate नहीं होता, कुछ dramatic तरीक़े से और condense नहीं होता — ये cell का अपना cargo move से पहले line up करना है।
Figure में arrangement देखिए। हर chromosome, हर एक अब भी दो chromatids का, एक central plane पर बैठा है। Spindle fibres दोनों poles से kinetochores तक जाते हैं।

Sequence ये है। अब nuclear envelope पूरी तरह जा चुका है, तो spindle fibres अंदर पहुँचकर हर chromosome के centromere पर बने kinetochores से attach हो सकते हैं। इस वाक्य की precision देखिए — fibres kinetochores से जुड़ते हैं, centromeres से नहीं, और chromosome arms से तो बिल्कुल नहीं।

फिर वो fibres सारे chromosomes को manoeuvre करके cell के equator पर ले आते हैं। वो plane ही metaphase plate है, जिसे equatorial plate भी कहते हैं। दोनों नाम सही हैं और दोनों question papers में आते हैं।

इतनी मेहनत करके line up क्यों करना? क्योंकि आगे जो होने वाला है उसकी वजह से। अगर हर chromosome midline पर बैठा हो और उसके दो chromatids opposite poles की तरफ़ मुँह किए हों, तो separation के वक़्त हर pole को हर chromosome से ठीक एक chromatid मिलेगा। Alignment ही split को fair बनाता है।
अब इस stage की एक दूसरी, बिल्कुल अलग property. Metaphase पर chromosomes सबसे ज़्यादा condensed होते हैं, और क्योंकि वो एक ही plane पर फैले हैं, सबसे कम overlapping होते हैं।

और यही वजह है कि chromosome morphology और number study करने के लिए metaphase सबसे अच्छा stage है। Karyotyping metaphase cells पर ठीक इसी वजह से की जाती है — maximally condensed, individually distinguishable.

<curious>पर रुकिए, interphase तो कहीं ज़्यादा लंबा है — वहाँ chromosomes क्यों नहीं study करते? क्योंकि criterion लंबाई नहीं, resolvability है। Interphase में chromatin decondensed और diffuse होता है, तो individual chromosomes resolve ही नहीं होते। Longest और most suitable दो अलग सवाल हैं, और N E E T इन्हें जानबूझकर साथ रखता है।

<text x="95" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">each chromatid is now a</text>
<text x="95" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">full daughter chromosome</text>

<text x="550" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">every pole receives one</text>
<text x="550" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">chromatid per chromosome</text>

board_events.text: The CENTROMERES SPLIT.
The two sister chromatids of each chromosome — now each a full-fledged daughter chromosome — are pulled to opposite poles.
Centromere leading, arms trailing.
This is the moment of equal partition.
Each pole now has a complete, identical chromosome set.
Anaphase is when chromosome number transiently APPEARS to rise — but no new DNA is made.

segments.text: Anaphase is short, it is decisive, and it is the stage examiners return to more than any other. Everything the cell has done so far was setup for this.
Watch what the figure shows. The chromatids that were paired on the plate are now single rods, travelling in opposite directions, and each pole is accumulating a complete set.
The trigger event, and I want it isolated on its own line, is this. The centromeres split. Up to this instant the sister chromatids were held together; from this instant they are not.

And the consequence follows immediately. The two sister chromatids of each chromosome are pulled to opposite poles. Note the promotion in status — the moment a chromatid gets its own centromere, it stops being a chromatid and becomes a full fledged daughter chromosome.

A small descriptive detail worth carrying, because it shows up in diagram based questions. They move centromere leading, arms trailing — which is why anaphase chromosomes are drawn as V or J shapes rather than straight rods.

This is the moment of equal partition. Everything before it was preparation, and everything after it is cleanup. If a question asks when the genetic material is actually divided, the answer is anaphase.
By the close of anaphase each pole has a complete, identical chromosome set. The equational promise we made three sections ago is kept right here, physically, by this movement.

One subtlety that traps people. Anaphase is the moment when the chromosome number appears to rise, because every chromatid now counts as its own chromosome. But notice — no new D N A is made here. Students who confuse chromatids separating with D N A doubling pick anaphase when the answer is S phase.
Anaphase छोटा है, decisive है, और examiners सबसे ज़्यादा इसी stage पर लौटते हैं। Cell ने अब तक जो किया वो सब इसी की setup थी।
Figure क्या दिखा रहा है, देखिए। जो chromatids plate पर paired थे वो अब single rods हैं, opposite directions में जा रहे हैं, और हर pole एक complete set जमा कर रहा है।
Trigger event, और मैं चाहता हूँ ये अपनी अलग line पर रहे, ये है। Centromeres split होते हैं। इस पल तक sister chromatids एक साथ पकड़े हुए थे; इस पल के बाद नहीं।

और नतीजा तुरंत आता है। हर chromosome के दोनों sister chromatids opposite poles की तरफ़ खींचे जाते हैं। Status में promotion देखिए — जिस पल chromatid को अपना centromere मिलता है, वो chromatid रहना छोड़ देता है और एक full fledged daughter chromosome बन जाता है।

एक छोटी descriptive detail जो साथ रखने लायक़ है, क्योंकि ये diagram-based questions में आती है। वो centromere आगे, arms पीछे की तरह चलते हैं — इसीलिए anaphase chromosomes को सीधी rods की जगह V या J shapes में draw किया जाता है।
यही equal partition का moment है। इससे पहले सब preparation था, इसके बाद सब cleanup है। अगर question पूछे कि genetic material असल में कब divide होता है, जवाब है anaphase.
Anaphase ख़त्म होते-होते हर pole के पास एक complete, identical chromosome set है। तीन sections पहले जो equational वादा हमने किया था, वो ठीक यहीं, physically, इसी movement से पूरा होता है।

एक subtlety जो लोगों को फँसाती है। Anaphase वो moment है जब chromosome number बढ़ता हुआ लगता है, क्योंकि अब हर chromatid अपना ख़ुद का chromosome गिना जाता है। पर ग़ौर कीजिए — यहाँ कोई नया D N A नहीं बनता। जो students chromatids के separate होने को D N A doubling समझ लेते हैं, वो anaphase चुन लेते हैं जबकि जवाब S phase है।

board_events.text: Having arrived at the poles, the chromosomes decondense back into chromatin.
Compact chromosomes were only ever needed for transport.
The nuclear envelope reassembles around each set.
The nucleolus, Golgi complex and endoplasmic reticulum reappear.
Two daughter nuclei now exist WITHIN ONE CELL — karyokinesis is complete.
Telophase is where the envelope REFORMS. Prophase is where it goes. Metaphase never touches it.

segments.text: Telophase is the easiest stage to learn, because it is simply prophase run backwards. Everything prophase took apart, telophase puts back.
Look carefully at the figure, and count the cells. Two nuclei — but one cell boundary. That distinction is the whole point of this stage.
First, the chromosomes, having arrived at the poles, decondense back into chromatin. They unwind. The compact rods you have been watching dissolve back into diffuse threads.

Why would the cell undo its own careful condensation? Because compact chromosomes were only ever needed for transport. Tightly wound D N A cannot be read or copied. Now that the cargo has arrived, it has to be unpacked to be useful again.
Second, the nuclear envelope reassembles around each of the two chromosome sets. Prophase dismantled it so the spindle could reach in; the spindle's work is done, so the envelope comes back.

Third, the rest of the list returns. The nucleolus, the Golgi complex and the endoplasmic reticulum all reappear. Compare that against the prophase list and you will see it is the same list, reversed.

And now the sentence that matters most. Two daughter nuclei now exist within one cell. Karyokinesis is complete — the nucleus has divided. But the cell has not. There is still one plasma membrane around the whole thing.
Fix the envelope timeline once and you are immune to a whole family of questions. Prophase takes the envelope down, by the end of prophase. Telophase puts it back. Metaphase never touches it.
Telophase सीखने में सबसे आसान stage है, क्योंकि ये बस prophase का उल्टा है। Prophase ने जो-जो तोड़ा था, telophase वो सब वापस जोड़ देता है।
Figure ध्यान से देखिए, और cells गिनिए। दो nuclei — पर cell boundary एक। यही distinction इस stage का पूरा point है।
पहले, chromosomes, poles पर पहुँचकर, decondense होकर वापस chromatin बन जाते हैं। वो खुल जाते हैं। जो compact rods आप देख रहे थे, वो वापस diffuse threads में घुल जाते हैं।

Cell अपनी ही careful condensation क्यों undo करेगा? क्योंकि compact chromosomes की ज़रूरत सिर्फ़ transport के लिए थी। कसकर लिपटा D N A ना पढ़ा जा सकता है ना copy किया जा सकता है। Cargo पहुँच गया, तो अब उसे unpack करना ही होगा ताकि वो फिर काम का बने।
दूसरा, nuclear envelope दोनों chromosome sets के चारों तरफ़ दोबारा assemble हो जाता है। Prophase ने उसे तोड़ा था ताकि spindle अंदर पहुँच सके; spindle का काम हो गया, तो envelope वापस आ जाता है।
तीसरा, बाक़ी list वापस आ जाती है। Nucleolus, Golgi complex और endoplasmic reticulum, सब दोबारा दिखने लगते हैं। इसे prophase वाली list से मिलाइए — वही list है, उल्टी।

और अब वो वाक्य जो सबसे ज़्यादा मायने रखता है। अब एक ही cell के अंदर दो daughter nuclei मौजूद हैं। Karyokinesis complete है — nucleus divide हो चुका। पर cell नहीं। पूरी चीज़ के चारों तरफ़ अब भी एक ही plasma membrane है।
Envelope की timeline एक बार fix कर लीजिए, फिर आप questions के पूरे परिवार से immune हैं। Prophase envelope को गिराता है, prophase के अंत तक। Telophase उसे वापस लगाता है। Metaphase उसे छूता तक नहीं।

board_events.text: ANIMAL CELLS: a CLEAVAGE FURROW forms by constriction of the plasma membrane.
It deepens from the periphery inward — wall $\to$ centre — until the cell pinches in two.
PLANT CELLS: the rigid cell wall FORBIDS pinching.
So a CELL PLATE is laid down from the centre outward — centre $\to$ wall — growing to fuse with the existing wall.
The middle lamella develops along this plate.
Karyokinesis without cytokinesis $\Rightarrow$ a multinucleate SYNCYTIUM — the liquid endosperm of a young coconut.
Furrow = ANIMAL (outside-in). Cell plate = PLANT (inside-out). This exact pair is a NEET staple.

segments.text: We left telophase with two nuclei inside one cell. Cytokinesis is what finally makes that one cell into two. And here plants and animals part ways.
The figure sets the two mechanisms side by side, and I want you to read them as answers to the same problem under different constraints. Same goal, different hardware.

In animal cells, a cleavage furrow forms by constriction of the plasma membrane. The membrane is flexible, so the cell can simply squeeze itself. Think of tightening a drawstring around the middle of a bag.
And the direction matters enormously. The furrow deepens from the periphery inward — from the wall toward the centre — until the cell pinches in two. Outside first, inside last.
Plant cells cannot do that. The rigid cell wall forbids pinching. You cannot tighten a drawstring around a wooden box. So the same job needs a completely different solution.

The plant's answer is to build rather than to squeeze. A cell plate is laid down from the centre outward — from the centre toward the wall — growing until it fuses with the existing wall and partitions the cell. Inside first, outside last. Exactly the opposite direction.
One associated fact to carry with it. The middle lamella develops along this plate. That is the layer that will end up cementing the two daughter cells together.

And when cytokinesis simply does not happen after karyokinesis, we get our syncytium — a multinucleate cell. The liquid endosperm of a young coconut is the classic example, and it is the one to quote.

<whisper>Let me say the exam line plainly. Furrow equals animal, outside in. Cell plate equals plant, inside out. This exact pair, swapped, is a N E E T staple — they will describe a furrow and call it a plant cell and wait for you to nod.
हमने telophase को एक ही cell में दो nuclei के साथ छोड़ा था। Cytokinesis वही है जो उस एक cell को आख़िरकार दो बनाता है। और यहीं plants और animals के रास्ते अलग हो जाते हैं।
Figure दोनों mechanisms को साथ-साथ रखता है, और मैं चाहता हूँ आप इन्हें एक ही problem के जवाब की तरह पढ़ें, अलग constraints के तहत। मक़सद वही, hardware अलग।
Animal cells में, plasma membrane के constriction से एक cleavage furrow बनता है। Membrane flexible है, तो cell बस अपने आप को दबा सकता है। एक थैले के बीच में drawstring कसने जैसा सोचिए।
और direction बहुत मायने रखती है। Furrow periphery से अंदर की तरफ़ गहरा होता है — wall से centre की ओर — जब तक cell दो हिस्सों में pinch ना हो जाए। पहले बाहर, आख़िर में अंदर।
Plant cells ऐसा नहीं कर सकते। Rigid cell wall pinching को मना करता है। लकड़ी के डिब्बे के चारों तरफ़ drawstring नहीं कसी जा सकती। तो वही काम एक बिल्कुल अलग solution माँगता है।

Plant का जवाब है दबाना नहीं, बनाना। एक cell plate centre से बाहर की तरफ़ बिछाई जाती है — centre से wall की ओर — बढ़ते हुए, जब तक वो existing wall से fuse होकर cell को बाँट ना दे। पहले अंदर, आख़िर में बाहर। बिल्कुल उल्टी direction.
इसके साथ एक जुड़ा हुआ fact भी रखिए। इसी plate के साथ middle lamella develop होती है। यही वो layer है जो आगे चलकर दोनों daughter cells को आपस में जोड़े रखेगी।
और जब karyokinesis के बाद cytokinesis होता ही नहीं, तो हमें अपना syncytium मिलता है — एक multinucleate cell. एक जवान नारियल का liquid endosperm classic example है, और यही quote करने लायक़ है।

<whisper>Exam line साफ़-साफ़ कह देता हूँ। Furrow मतलब animal, बाहर से अंदर। Cell plate मतलब plant, अंदर से बाहर। यही जोड़ी, उलटी करके, N E E T का staple है — वो furrow describe करेंगे और उसे plant cell कहेंगे, और इंतज़ार करेंगे कि आप सिर हिला दें।

board_events.text: 1. Growth and development of a multicellular body from the single-celled zygote.
2. Faithful maintenance of chromosome number and genetic identity across all body cells.
3. Restoration of the proper nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio — cell-size control.
4. Repair, wound-healing and regeneration of worn or lost parts; and multiplication in unicellular organisms.
The same engine, with the check points removed, becomes uncontrolled proliferation.
When mitosis escapes its check points: uncontrolled proliferation — the basis of tumours and cancer.

segments.text: We have walked the mechanism end to end. Now step back and ask the question a Board examiner asks — what is all of this actually for?
The figure fans out four functions from one process, and then adds the failure mode underneath. Learn the four, and learn the fifth thing that happens when the four go wrong.
One. Growth and development of a multicellular body from the single celled zygote. Every cell in your body traces back through mitotic divisions to one fertilised egg.
Two. Faithful maintenance of chromosome number and genetic identity across all body cells. This is the equational property doing its work at the scale of an entire organism.

Three, and this one gets forgotten. Restoration of the proper nucleo cytoplasmic ratio. A cell that grows too large has too much cytoplasm for one nucleus to service; dividing restores the balance. So mitosis is also cell size control.

Four. Repair, wound healing and regeneration of worn or lost parts. And add one more for the unicellular world — in single celled organisms, mitosis is simply how they multiply. For them, division is reproduction.

Now the flip side, and it follows directly from the check point section. Every one of those benefits depends on the gates working. Remove the gates and the engine does not stop — it just stops asking permission.

When mitosis escapes its check points, the result is uncontrolled proliferation, and that is the basis of tumours and cancer. The same process that builds a body from one cell can dismantle it, and the only difference is regulation.
हमने mechanism को शुरू से आख़िर तक चला लिया। अब पीछे हटकर वो सवाल पूछिए जो Board examiner पूछता है — ये सब आख़िर है किस लिए?
Figure एक process से चार functions निकालता है, और फिर नीचे failure mode जोड़ देता है। चारों सीखिए, और वो पाँचवीं चीज़ भी जो तब होती है जब ये चारों बिगड़ जाएँ।
एक. Single celled zygote से एक multicellular body का growth और development. आपके शरीर का हर cell mitotic divisions से होते हुए एक fertilised egg तक पहुँचता है।
दो. सारे body cells में chromosome number और genetic identity का faithful maintenance. ये equational property है जो पूरे organism के scale पर काम कर रही है।

तीन, और यही भूल जाया जाता है। सही nucleo cytoplasmic ratio की restoration. जो cell बहुत बड़ा हो जाए, उसमें एक nucleus के संभालने के लिए cytoplasm ज़्यादा हो जाता है; divide करना संतुलन लौटा देता है। तो mitosis cell size control भी है।

चार. Repair, wound healing, और घिसे या खोए हुए parts का regeneration. और unicellular दुनिया के लिए एक और जोड़ लीजिए — single celled organisms में mitosis ही उनके बढ़ने का तरीक़ा है। उनके लिए division ही reproduction है।
अब दूसरा पहलू, जो सीधे check point वाले section से निकलता है। इनमें से हर फ़ायदा इस बात पर टिका है कि gates काम कर रहे हों। Gates हटा दीजिए और engine रुकता नहीं — बस इजाज़त माँगना छोड़ देता है।

जब mitosis अपने check points से बच निकलता है, नतीजा है uncontrolled proliferation, और यही tumours और cancer की बुनियाद है। जो process एक cell से पूरा शरीर बनाता है, वही उसे तोड़ भी सकता है — और फ़र्क़ सिर्फ़ regulation का है।

sections.title: Worked Example 1 — tracking DNA against chromosome number

board_events.text: Worked Example 1 [CBSE Board level]
A cell in G1 phase has 24 chromosomes and a DNA content of 12 picograms.
Find: (a) chromosome number and DNA content at the END OF S PHASE; (b) in each daughter cell at the END OF MITOSIS.

board_events.text: RULE: S phase doubles the DNA, NOT the chromosome number.
(a) End of S phase: chromosomes = 24 (unchanged); DNA $= 12 \times 2 = 24$ pg. Each chromosome now has two sister chromatids.
(b) Mitosis is equational, and the duplicated DNA is split equally. Each daughter: chromosomes = 24; DNA = 12 pg.
Presentation point: always STATE THE RULE you are applying before substituting — examiners award method marks.

segments.text: Our first worked example is the Board's favourite shape for this chapter — a small numerical that is really a concept check in disguise.
A cell in G one phase has twenty four chromosomes and a D N A content of twelve picograms. That is our starting state, and notice we are given both quantities — that is the tell.
We are asked for two things. Part a, the chromosome number and D N A content at the end of S phase. Part b, the same two quantities in each daughter cell at the end of mitosis.
Before substituting anything, set up the table you see here. Stage down the left, chromosome number in one column, D N A in another. The discipline of the layout is doing half the work.
Now state the rule before you touch a number. S phase doubles the D N A, not the chromosome number. Everything in part a falls out of that one sentence.

So part a. At the end of S phase the chromosome number is twenty four — unchanged. The D N A is twelve times two, which is twenty four picograms. And each of those twenty four chromosomes now consists of two sister chromatids. Say that last part explicitly; it earns the mark.

Part b. Mitosis is equational, and the duplicated D N A is split equally between the two daughters. So each daughter gets twenty four chromosomes and twelve picograms of D N A — right back to the G one value. That return to baseline is the signature of a mitotic cycle.

One presentation point that is worth actual marks. Always state the rule you are applying before you substitute. Writing S phase doubles D N A, not chromosome number, and then substituting, earns method marks even if you slip on arithmetic.
हमारा पहला worked example इस chapter के लिए Board का पसंदीदा shape है — एक छोटा numerical जो असल में भेस बदला हुआ concept check है।
G one phase में एक cell के पास twenty four chromosomes हैं और D N A content है twelve picograms. यही हमारी starting state है, और ग़ौर कीजिए हमें दोनों quantities दी गई हैं — यही इशारा है।
हमसे दो चीज़ें पूछी गई हैं। Part a, S phase के अंत में chromosome number और D N A content. Part b, mitosis के अंत में हर daughter cell में वही दो quantities.
कुछ भी substitute करने से पहले, यहाँ जो table दिख रही है वो बना लीजिए। बाईं तरफ़ stage, एक column में chromosome number, दूसरे में D N A. Layout का ये discipline ही आधा काम कर रहा है।
अब किसी number को छूने से पहले rule बोलिए। S phase D N A को double करता है, chromosome number को नहीं। Part a का सब कुछ इसी एक वाक्य से निकल आता है।

तो part a. S phase के अंत में chromosome number है twenty four — unchanged. D N A है twelve into two, यानी twenty four picograms. और उन twenty four chromosomes में से हर एक अब दो sister chromatids का है। ये आख़िरी हिस्सा explicitly लिखिए; इसी का mark मिलता है।

Part b. Mitosis equational है, और duplicated D N A दोनों daughters में equally बँटता है। तो हर daughter को twenty four chromosomes और twelve picograms D N A मिलते हैं — बिल्कुल वापस G one वाली value पर। Baseline पर ये लौटना ही mitotic cycle की पहचान है।

एक presentation point जिसके सचमुच marks मिलते हैं। Substitute करने से पहले हमेशा वो rule लिखिए जो आप apply कर रहे हैं। S phase doubles D N A, not chromosome number लिखकर फिर substitute करना — arithmetic में चूक भी जाएँ तो method marks मिल जाते हैं।

sections.title: Worked Example 2 — ordering the whole cycle

board_events.text: Worked Example 2 [CUET level]
Arrange in the correct chronological order of the cell cycle: Anaphase, G1, Metaphase, S, Telophase, Prophase, G2.
Step 1: Interphase precedes M phase.
Step 2: within interphase the order is $G_1 \to S \to G_2$.
Step 3: within mitosis the order is Prophase $\to$ Metaphase $\to$ Anaphase $\to$ Telophase.

board_events.text: Correct order: G1 $\to$ S $\to$ G2 $\to$ Prophase $\to$ Metaphase $\to$ Anaphase $\to$ Telophase.
Speed tip: the mnemonic PMAT locks the four mitotic stages; everything else simply slots in FRONT of it.

segments.text: C U E T loves crisp ordering questions, and this is the archetype. It looks like pure recall, but there is a technique that makes it instant.
Arrange the following in correct chronological order of the cell cycle. Anaphase, G one, Metaphase, S, Telophase, Prophase, G two. Seven items, deliberately shuffled.
Step one, and this is the coarse cut. Interphase precedes M phase. That immediately splits your seven items into two groups — the three interphase items, then the four mitotic ones.
Step two. Within interphase the order is G one, then S, then G two. Notice the logic of the naming — the two gaps bracket the synthesis. Gap one, synthesise, gap two.
Step three. Within mitosis the order is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. If you have P M A T you already have this half for free.
Assemble it as the figure shows. The interphase block on the left, the P M A T block on the right, and the boundary between them is where the cell stops preparing and starts dividing.
So the correct order is G one, S, G two, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Seven items, and every one of them placed by two rules rather than by memory of the list.

The speed tip to carry out of here. P M A T locks the four mitotic stages permanently. Then everything else simply slots in front of it. You are never ordering seven things — you are ordering three, in front of a block you already know.
C U E T को crisp ordering questions पसंद हैं, और ये उनका archetype है। दिखने में pure recall लगता है, पर एक technique है जो इसे instant बना देती है।
इन्हें cell cycle के सही chronological order में लगाइए। Anaphase, G one, Metaphase, S, Telophase, Prophase, G two. सात items, जानबूझकर shuffle किए हुए।
Step one, और ये coarse cut है। Interphase M phase से पहले आता है। इससे आपके सात items तुरंत दो groups में बँट जाते हैं — तीन interphase वाले, फिर चार mitotic.
Step two. Interphase के अंदर order है G one, फिर S, फिर G two. Naming का logic देखिए — दोनों gaps synthesis को घेरे हुए हैं। Gap one, synthesise, gap two.
Step three. Mitosis के अंदर order है prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. अगर आपके पास P M A T है तो ये आधा हिस्सा मुफ़्त में मिल गया।
Figure जैसा दिखा रहा है वैसे assemble कीजिए। बाईं तरफ़ interphase block, दाईं तरफ़ P M A T block, और उनके बीच की boundary वो है जहाँ cell तैयारी छोड़कर divide करना शुरू करता है।
तो सही order है G one, S, G two, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. सात items, और हर एक को list याद करके नहीं, दो rules से जगह मिली।

यहाँ से जो speed tip लेकर जाना है। P M A T चारों mitotic stages को permanently lock कर देता है। फिर बाक़ी सब बस उसके आगे slot हो जाता है। आप कभी सात चीज़ें order नहीं कर रहे — आप तीन order कर रहे हैं, एक ऐसे block के आगे जो आपको पहले से आता है।

board_events.text: A $\to$ (iii) Metaphase — alignment on the metaphase plate.
B $\to$ (i) Anaphase — centromere splitting and chromatid separation are the defining anaphase events.
C $\to$ (ii) Telophase; D $\to$ (iv) Prophase — reassembly reverses exactly what condensation began.
Answer: A-iii, B-i, C-ii, D-iv

segments.text: Match the column items are how NEET tests whether you know each stage by its signature event, rather than as a blur of descriptions.
Column one, item A — chromosomes align at the equator. Item B — centromeres split, and chromatids move to the poles.
Item C — the nuclear envelope reforms and chromosomes decondense. Item D — chromatin condenses and the spindle begins to form.
And the four options, deliberately out of order. Anaphase, telophase, metaphase, prophase. Never assume the options are listed in the sequence they occur — they almost never are.
Work it by signature event, one at a time, as the arrows in the figure do. Do not read the whole thing and guess — take each item and ask what one word it belongs to.
A goes to metaphase. Alignment on the metaphase plate is the defining metaphase event — the word equator should fire metaphase in your head instantly.
B goes to anaphase. Centromere splitting and chromatid separation are the defining anaphase events. If a question mentions centromeres splitting, the answer is anaphase and nothing else.

C goes to telophase, D goes to prophase. And notice how neatly those two pair up. Telophase reassembles and decondenses; prophase condenses and dismantles. C and D are the same events, run in opposite directions.
So the answer is A three, B one, C two, D four. Every one of them decided by a single signature event rather than by weighing whole descriptions against each other.
Match the column items वो तरीक़ा है जिससे N E E T जाँचता है कि आप हर stage को उसके signature event से पहचानते हैं, या बस descriptions के धुँधलके की तरह।
Column one, item A — chromosomes equator पर align होते हैं। Item B — centromeres split होते हैं, और chromatids poles की तरफ़ जाते हैं।
Item C — nuclear envelope दोबारा बनता है और chromosomes decondense होते हैं। Item D — chromatin condense होता है और spindle बनना शुरू होता है।
और चार options, जानबूझकर बेतरतीब। Anaphase, telophase, metaphase, prophase. कभी मत मानिए कि options उसी sequence में लिखे हैं जिसमें वो होते हैं — लगभग कभी नहीं होते।
Signature event से एक-एक करके काम कीजिए, जैसे figure के arrows कर रहे हैं। पूरा पढ़कर अंदाज़ा मत लगाइए — हर item लीजिए और पूछिए ये किस एक शब्द का है।
A जाता है metaphase पर। Metaphase plate पर alignment ही metaphase का defining event है — equator शब्द आपके दिमाग़ में तुरंत metaphase जगा देना चाहिए।
B जाता है anaphase पर। Centromere splitting और chromatid separation anaphase के defining events हैं। अगर question में centromeres का splitting आए, जवाब anaphase है और कुछ नहीं।

C जाता है telophase पर, D जाता है prophase पर। और देखिए ये दोनों कितने साफ़ जोड़े बनाते हैं। Telophase reassemble और decondense करता है; prophase condense और dismantle करता है। C और D वही events हैं, उल्टी direction में चलते हुए।
तो जवाब है A three, B one, C two, D four. इनमें से हर एक एक single signature event से तय हुआ, ना कि पूरी descriptions को आपस में तौलकर।

A single cell from the tip of an onion root divides repeatedly by mitosis. How many successive mitotic divisions are required to produce 128 cells?

Each mitotic division doubles the number of cells. After $n$ divisions, the number of cells is $2^n$.
