<text x="534" y="88" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">1. HALVES the chromosome number</text>
<text x="534" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="10" fill="#6b7280">during gamete / spore formation</text>
<text x="534" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">2. MAINTAINS the count across</text>
<text x="534" y="138" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">generations</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Significance 2: this MAINTAINS chromosome-number constancy across generations of sexually reproducing organisms.
Fertilisation doubles. Only meiosis can pay it back.
Without the halving, each generation would double: 2n becomes 4n, then 8n, then 16n.
So 'halving' and 'constancy' are not in conflict — the halving is what BUYS the constancy.
A question asking 'how is chromosome number kept constant across generations?' wants BOTH halves: meiosis halves, fertilisation restores.

segments.text: <curious>Here is a claim that sounds self contradictory until you follow the arithmetic. Meiosis halves the chromosome number — and that halving is precisely what keeps the number constant. How can both be true?

Significance one, and it is the mechanism. Meiosis halves the chromosome number during gamete or spore formation. Two n becomes n. We have watched exactly where this happens — anaphase one, when the homologues disjoin.

Now follow the cycle in the figure. Parent body, two n. Meiosis halves it to n — the gamete. Two gametes fuse at fertilisation, n plus n, giving two n — the zygote. Look at the two ends of that dashed line. Same number.

Significance two is the consequence. This maintains chromosome number constancy across generations of sexually reproducing organisms. The halving in gamete formation is balanced by the doubling at fertilisation. They cancel.

That is the way to hold it. Fertilisation doubles — that is not optional, that is what fertilisation is. Two cells fuse into one. So something has to pay that back before the next fertilisation, and only meiosis can.

Run the counterfactual, because it makes the necessity obvious. Without the halving, each generation would double. Two n becomes four n, then eight n, then sixteen n. Within a handful of generations the arithmetic is absurd, and the lineage is finished.

So halving and constancy are not in conflict at all. The halving is what buys the constancy. It is not that meiosis keeps the number the same; it is that meiosis and fertilisation together keep it the same, and meiosis is the half that goes down.

So a question asking how chromosome number is kept constant across generations wants both halves of that sentence. Meiosis halves, fertilisation restores. Give only one and you have described a process that runs away in one direction.

<curious>ये रहा एक दावा जो अपने आप में विरोधाभासी लगता है, जब तक आप arithmetic ना चलाएँ। Meiosis chromosome number को आधा करता है — और वही halving number को constant रखती है। दोनों एक साथ सच कैसे हो सकते हैं?

पहली significance, और यही mechanism है। Meiosis, gamete या spore formation के दौरान chromosome number को आधा करता है। Two n से n. हमने ठीक-ठीक देखा है ये कहाँ होता है — anaphase one में, जब homologues disjoin होते हैं।

अब figure में cycle follow कीजिए। Parent body, two n. Meiosis उसे आधा करके n कर देता है — gamete. दो gametes fertilisation पर fuse होते हैं, n plus n, और two n बनता है — zygote. उस dashed line के दोनों सिरे देखिए। वही number.

दूसरी significance नतीजा है। ये sexually reproducing organisms की generations के आर-पार chromosome number की constancy बनाए रखती है। Gamete formation में जो halving है, वो fertilisation के doubling से balance हो जाती है। दोनों कट जाते हैं।

इसे इस तरह पकड़िए। Fertilisation double करता है — ये optional नहीं है, fertilisation है ही यही। दो cells मिलकर एक बनते हैं। तो अगले fertilisation से पहले किसी को वो चुकाना है, और सिर्फ़ meiosis चुका सकता है।

Counterfactual चलाइए, क्योंकि उससे ज़रूरत साफ़ हो जाती है। बिना halving के, हर generation double होती जाती। Two n से four n, फिर eight n, फिर sixteen n. कुछ ही generations में arithmetic बेतुका हो जाता, और वंश ख़त्म।

तो halving और constancy में कोई टकराव है ही नहीं। Halving ही constancy ख़रीदती है। ऐसा नहीं कि meiosis number को वही रखता है; बात ये है कि meiosis और fertilisation मिलकर उसे वही रखते हैं, और meiosis वो आधा है जो नीचे जाता है।

तो जो सवाल पूछे कि generations के आर-पार chromosome number constant कैसे रहता है, उसे उस वाक्य के दोनों आधे हिस्से चाहिए। Meiosis halves, fertilisation restores. सिर्फ़ एक दीजिए और आपने एक ऐसा process बताया जो एक ही दिशा में भागता जाता है।

sections.title: Significance 3 — variation, and the link to evolution

board_events.text: Crossing over: Pachytene of Meiosis I. Independent assortment: Metaphase I.
BOTH sources are MEIOSIS I events. Meiosis II adds no new variation at all.
Together they ensure the four cells are genetically DISTINCT — the raw material of biological variation.
This increase in genetic variability from one generation to the next is why meiosis matters for EVOLUTION.
The variation meiosis generates is what natural selection ACTS UPON.
So the three points together: halve, keep constant, and vary.

segments.text: The third significance is the one that connects this chapter to the whole of the rest of biology.

Meiosis generates genetic variation, through two mechanisms — crossing over, and independent assortment. Name both. A question asking for the sources of variation in meiosis wants two answers, not one.
Two boxes on the left feeding one box in the middle, feeding natural selection on the right. And note the stage labels on those two boxes — pachytene, and metaphase one.
Be precise about where each one lives. Crossing over happens in pachytene of Meiosis one. Independent assortment happens at metaphase one. Exam questions ask for the stage, not just the name.

And note carefully — both sources are Meiosis one events. Meiosis two merely separates chromatids and adds no new variation at all. So a question asking where the variation among the four cells arises has exactly one answer, and it is Meiosis one.
Together the two mechanisms ensure the four cells are genetically distinct. That is the raw material of biological variation. Four cells from one meiocyte, and no two of them the same.

And this increase in genetic variability from one generation to the next is, in fact, why meiosis matters for evolution. That phrasing is worth learning, because it is how the point is usually framed.

The link is this. Natural selection can only choose among differences. If every offspring were identical, selection would have nothing to select between — it would be a sorting process with nothing to sort. The variation meiosis generates is what selection acts upon.

So hold the three points together as three verbs. Halve. Keep constant. And vary. Halving is the mechanism, constancy is what it buys across generations, and variation is what it buys for the species. A five mark significance question wants all three.
तीसरी significance वही है जो इस chapter को बाक़ी पूरी biology से जोड़ती है।
Meiosis genetic variation पैदा करता है, दो mechanisms से — crossing over, और independent assortment. दोनों का नाम लीजिए। जो सवाल meiosis में variation के sources पूछे, उसे दो जवाब चाहिए, एक नहीं।
बाईं तरफ़ दो boxes बीच वाले एक box में जाते हैं, और वो दाईं तरफ़ natural selection में। और उन दोनों boxes पर stage labels देखिए — pachytene, और metaphase one.
हर एक कहाँ रहता है, इस पर precise रहिए। Crossing over, Meiosis one के pachytene में होता है। Independent assortment, metaphase one पर होता है। Exam सवाल stage पूछते हैं, सिर्फ़ नाम नहीं।

और ध्यान से देखिए — दोनों sources Meiosis one के events हैं। Meiosis two बस chromatids अलग करता है और कोई नई variation जोड़ता ही नहीं। तो जो सवाल पूछे कि चारों cells में variation कहाँ पैदा होती है, उसका ठीक एक जवाब है, और वो है Meiosis one.
दोनों mechanisms मिलकर पक्का करते हैं कि चारों cells genetically distinct हों। यही biological variation का कच्चा माल है। एक meiocyte से चार cells, और कोई दो एक जैसे नहीं।

और एक generation से अगली तक genetic variability का यही बढ़ना, दरअसल, वो वजह है कि meiosis evolution के लिए मायने रखता है। ये phrasing सीखने लायक़ है, क्योंकि आमतौर पर यही तरीक़ा है जिससे बात रखी जाती है।

कड़ी ये है। Natural selection सिर्फ़ फ़र्क़ों में से चुन सकता है। अगर हर offspring एक जैसा होता, तो selection के पास चुनने को कुछ होता ही नहीं — वो एक ऐसा sorting process होता जिसके पास sort करने को कुछ नहीं। Meiosis जो variation पैदा करता है, selection उसी पर काम करता है।

तो तीनों points को तीन verbs की तरह पकड़िए। Halve. Keep constant. और vary. Halving mechanism है, constancy वो है जो generations के आर-पार मिलती है, और variation वो जो species को मिलती है। पाँच marks का significance वाला सवाल तीनों माँगता है।

board_events.text: (a) End of Meiosis I (REDUCTIONAL): chromosome number $= n = 9$; each chromosome still has TWO chromatids.
(b) End of Meiosis II (EQUATIONAL): chromosome number $= 9$; each chromosome now has ONE chromatid.
Notice: between (a) and (b) the chromosome number did NOT change. Only the chromatid count did.
Presentation point: track chromosome number and chromatids per chromosome in TWO SEPARATE COLUMNS.

segments.text: The Board's standard numerical for this subtopic. It looks like two questions but it is really one question about which column moves when.

A diploid plant meiocyte has two n equals eighteen chromosomes. So the haploid number, n, is nine. Work that out before you go any further — half of eighteen is nine, and that nine is going to appear in both answers.

State, for one resulting cell, the chromosome number and the number of chromatids per chromosome. Part a, at the end of Meiosis one. Part b, at the end of Meiosis two. Note it wants two quantities each time, not one.
Set up the two columns before substituting anything. Chromosome number in one, chromatids per chromosome in the other. The layout does the thinking for you.

Part a. End of Meiosis one, which is reductional. The chromosome number is n, which is nine. And each chromosome still has two chromatids, because the centromeres have not split. State that reason — it is where the mark is.

Part b. End of Meiosis two, which is equational. The chromosome number is still nine — unchanged, because equational divisions conserve the number. And now each chromosome has one chromatid, because the centromeres have split and the chromatids separated.

Now look at what happened between part a and part b. The chromosome number did not change — nine and nine. Only the chromatid count changed — two and one. If your answer has nine going to four point five, you have applied the reduction twice.

The presentation point, and it is the same one as part one of this chapter. Track chromosome number and chromatids per chromosome in two separate columns. Meiosis one changes the number. Meiosis two changes the chromatids. Never both at once.
इस subtopic के लिए Board का standard numerical. दिखने में दो सवाल हैं पर असल में ये एक ही सवाल है — कौन सा column कब हिलता है।

एक diploid plant meiocyte में two n बराबर eighteen chromosomes हैं। तो haploid number, n, है nine. आगे बढ़ने से पहले ये निकाल लीजिए — eighteen का आधा nine है, और वही nine दोनों जवाबों में आने वाला है।

एक बनने वाले cell के लिए बताइए chromosome number और हर chromosome में chromatids की संख्या। Part a, Meiosis one के अंत में। Part b, Meiosis two के अंत में। ग़ौर कीजिए हर बार उसे दो quantities चाहिए, एक नहीं।
कुछ भी substitute करने से पहले दो columns बना लीजिए। एक में chromosome number, दूसरे में हर chromosome के chromatids. Layout आपके लिए सोचने का काम कर देता है।
Part a. Meiosis one का अंत, जो reductional है। Chromosome number है n, यानी nine. और हर chromosome में अब भी दो chromatids हैं, क्योंकि centromeres split नहीं हुए। ये वजह लिखिए — mark वहीं है।

Part b. Meiosis two का अंत, जो equational है। Chromosome number अब भी nine है — unchanged, क्योंकि equational divisions number को बचाए रखते हैं। और अब हर chromosome में एक chromatid है, क्योंकि centromeres split हो गए और chromatids अलग हो गए।

अब देखिए part a और part b के बीच क्या हुआ। Chromosome number बदला ही नहीं — nine और nine. सिर्फ़ chromatid count बदला — दो और एक। अगर आपके जवाब में nine से four point five हो रहा है, तो आपने reduction दो बार लगा दिया है।

Presentation point, और ये वही है जो इस chapter के part one में था। Chromosome number और हर chromosome के chromatids को दो अलग columns में track कीजिए। Meiosis one number बदलता है। Meiosis two chromatids बदलता है। कभी दोनों एक साथ नहीं।

board_events.text: Number of meiocytes $= \dfrac{60}{4} = 15$
General rule: meiocytes needed = cells required $\div$ 4.
Why 4 and not $2^n$? Because meiosis is a fixed, one-off process — it is not repeated doublings.
Trap to avoid: this 1-to-4 ratio holds for SPORE and POLLEN formation. Do not apply it blindly to animal egg formation.

segments.text: A C U E T counting question. It is one division sum, and the entire difficulty is knowing which number to divide by.
How many meiotic divisions, meaning meiocytes undergoing complete meiosis, are required to produce sixty pollen grains?
State the rule first. One complete meiosis of a single meiocyte — here a pollen mother cell — yields four haploid cells. That is a microspore tetrad, which goes on to become four pollen grains.
One pollen mother cell, one complete meiosis, four pollen grains. That is the unit of the whole calculation, and once you have it the sum is trivial.
So the number of meiocytes is sixty divided by four, which is fifteen. Fifteen meiotic divisions are required. One line of arithmetic, resting entirely on the one to four ratio.

Generalise it. Meiocytes needed equals cells required divided by four. Contrast that with part one of this chapter, where mitotic counting used two to the power n. Different process, different rule — do not reach for the wrong one.

And it is worth knowing why the two rules differ. Mitosis repeats — a cell divides, and both daughters can divide again, so the count compounds as two to the power n. Meiosis does not repeat. It is a fixed, one off process that runs once and yields exactly four. So you divide by four; you do not take a logarithm.

And the trap the question is set around. This one to four ratio holds for spore and pollen formation. Do not apply it blindly to animal egg formation, where the yield differs. Notice the question said pollen grains — that word is what licensed the division by four.
एक C U E T counting सवाल। ये एक ही division का सवाल है, और पूरी मुश्किल ये जानने में है कि किस number से भाग देना है।
Sixty pollen grains बनाने के लिए कितने meiotic divisions चाहिए, यानी कितने meiocytes जो पूरा meiosis करें?
पहले rule लिखिए। एक अकेले meiocyte का एक पूरा meiosis — यहाँ एक pollen mother cell — चार haploid cells देता है। यही microspore tetrad है, जो आगे चलकर चार pollen grains बनता है।
एक pollen mother cell, एक पूरा meiosis, चार pollen grains. यही पूरे calculation की unit है, और ये मिल जाए तो सवाल मामूली है।
तो meiocytes की संख्या है sixty divided by four, यानी fifteen. Fifteen meiotic divisions चाहिए। Arithmetic की एक line, जो पूरी तरह one to four ratio पर टिकी है।

इसे generalise कीजिए। Meiocytes चाहिए बराबर cells required divided by four. इसे इस chapter के part one से मिलाइए, जहाँ mitotic counting two to the power n इस्तेमाल करती थी। अलग process, अलग rule — ग़लत वाला मत उठाइए।

और ये जानना ज़रूरी है कि दोनों rules अलग क्यों हैं। Mitosis दोहराता है — एक cell divide होता है, और दोनों daughters फिर divide कर सकती हैं, तो count two to the power n की तरह compound होता है। Meiosis दोहराता नहीं। वो एक तय, एक-बारगी process है जो एक बार चलता है और ठीक चार देता है। तो आप चार से भाग देते हैं; logarithm नहीं लेते।

और वो trap जिसके इर्द-गिर्द सवाल बना है। ये one to four ratio spore और pollen formation के लिए टिकता है। Animal egg formation पर इसे आँख मूँदकर मत लगाइए, जहाँ yield अलग है। ग़ौर कीजिए सवाल ने pollen grains कहा — उसी शब्द ने चार से भाग देने की इजाज़त दी।

board_events.text: A $\to$ (ii). Anaphase I separates HOMOLOGUES.
B $\to$ (i). Anaphase II separates SISTER CHROMATIDS.
C $\to$ (iv). Meiosis I is REDUCTIONAL. D $\to$ (iii). Meiosis II is EQUATIONAL.
Answer: A-ii, B-i, C-iv, D-iii

segments.text: This match the column is built entirely on the reductional-equational pairing, and it is beautifully symmetrical — two anaphases and two divisions.
Column one. A, anaphase one. B, anaphase two. C, Meiosis one. D, Meiosis two. Notice A and B are stages, while C and D are whole divisions. The paper is testing both levels at once.
Column two. One, sister chromatids separate. Two, homologous chromosomes separate. Three, equational division. Four, reductional division.
Look at the arrows and notice the pattern — every single one crosses. The options were deliberately laid out so that the naive straight-across answer is wrong in all four rows.
A goes to two. Anaphase one separates homologues. Not chromatids. This is the point we have hammered throughout, and here it is again as a one mark decision.
B goes to one. Anaphase two separates sister chromatids. So A and B take the two separation options between them, and they take them the opposite way round from how they are listed.

C goes to four. Meiosis one is reductional. D goes to three. Meiosis two is equational. And notice these two follow directly from A and B — separating homologues is what makes a division reductional, and separating chromatids is what makes it equational.

So the answer is A two, B one, C four, D three. Every option crossed, which is a good reminder never to assume the columns line up. And you only really had to know one thing — what separates in each anaphase. The rest followed.
ये match the column पूरी तरह reductional-equational जोड़ी पर बना है, और ख़ूबसूरती से symmetrical है — दो anaphases और दो divisions.
Column one. A, anaphase one. B, anaphase two. C, Meiosis one. D, Meiosis two. ग़ौर कीजिए A और B stages हैं, जबकि C और D पूरे divisions. Paper दोनों levels एक साथ जाँच रहा है।
Column two. One, sister chromatids separate. Two, homologous chromosomes separate. Three, equational division. Four, reductional division.
Arrows देखिए और pattern पर ग़ौर कीजिए — हर एक cross करता है। Options जानबूझकर ऐसे रखे गए हैं कि सीधा आर-पार वाला भोला जवाब चारों rows में ग़लत हो।
A जाता है two पर। Anaphase one homologues को separate करता है। Chromatids को नहीं। यही वो point है जिस पर हम शुरू से हथौड़ा मार रहे हैं, और यहाँ वो फिर एक mark के फ़ैसले की शक्ल में है।

B जाता है one पर। Anaphase two sister chromatids को separate करता है। तो A और B दोनों separation वाले options आपस में बाँट लेते हैं, और वो उन्हें उल्टे क्रम में लेते हैं, जिस क्रम में वो लिखे हैं उससे।

C जाता है four पर। Meiosis one reductional है। D जाता है three पर। Meiosis two equational है। और ग़ौर कीजिए ये दोनों सीधे A और B से निकलते हैं — homologues को अलग करना ही division को reductional बनाता है, और chromatids को अलग करना उसे equational.

तो जवाब है A two, B one, C four, D three. हर option cross हुआ, जो अच्छी याद दिलाता है कि कभी मत मानिए columns सीधे मिलते हैं। और आपको असल में सिर्फ़ एक चीज़ जाननी थी — हर anaphase में क्या separate होता है। बाक़ी अपने आप निकल आया।

sections.title: Worked Example 4 — the interkinesis assertion-reason

board_events.text: Worked Example 4 [NEET high-difficulty, assertion-reason]
Assertion (A): No DNA replication occurs between Meiosis I and Meiosis II.
Reason (R): The chromosomes entering Meiosis II already consist of two sister chromatids each.

board_events.caption: Three questions, not two

<text x="320" y="242" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Answer: (a) both true, and R IS the correct explanation of A</text>

board_events.text: Step 1 — A is TRUE. Interkinesis lacks an S phase.
Step 2 — R is TRUE. The chromatids were produced by the SINGLE replication that preceded Meiosis I.
Step 3 — does R EXPLAIN A? This is the step that decides the mark.
YES — since the duplicated chromatids are already present and only need SEPARATING, no further replication is required.
Answer: (a) both true, and R IS the correct explanation of A.

segments.text: Our last worked example, and it is the mirror image of the one in the last part. There, the reason was false. Here, both statements are true — and the whole question turns on the third step.
Assertion. No D N A replication occurs between Meiosis one and Meiosis two.
Reason. The chromosomes entering Meiosis two already consist of two sister chromatids each. Both statements should look familiar — we did both in the interkinesis section.
Three steps, and the figure lays them out as three separate judgements. Is A true. Is R true. And then the one that decides the mark.
Step one. A is true. Interkinesis lacks an S phase. Straightforward, and we established it directly.

Step two. R is true, judged on its own. The chromatids were produced by the single replication that preceded Meiosis one, so each chromosome enters Meiosis two already duplicated. Also plainly correct.

Step three, and this is where the mark actually is. Does R explain A? Two trues do not settle it — you have to ask whether the second sentence is the reason for the first, or just a true fact standing nearby.

And the answer is yes, directly. Since the duplicated chromatids are already present and only need separating, no further replication is required. R is not a coincidence sitting next to A — R is why A is true. Indeed, replicating again would defeat the reduction entirely.

So the answer is A — both true, and R is the correct explanation. Compare this with the assertion reason in the last part, where the answer was A true, R false. Same three step method, different verdict. The method is what you carry; the verdict changes every time.
हमारा आख़िरी worked example, और ये पिछले part वाले का आईना है। वहाँ reason झूठा था। यहाँ दोनों statements सच हैं — और पूरा सवाल तीसरे step पर टिका है।
Assertion. Meiosis one और Meiosis two के बीच कोई D N A replication नहीं होता।
Reason. Meiosis two में घुसते chromosomes पहले से दो-दो sister chromatids के हैं। दोनों statements जाने-पहचाने लगने चाहिए — हमने दोनों interkinesis वाले section में किए थे।
तीन steps, और figure उन्हें तीन अलग फ़ैसलों की तरह रखता है। क्या A सच है। क्या R सच है। और फिर वो जो mark तय करता है।
Step one. A सच है। Interkinesis में S phase नहीं होता। सीधा, और हमने इसे सीधे स्थापित किया था।
Step two. R सच है, अकेले में जाँचकर। Chromatids उस एक replication से बने जो Meiosis one से पहले हुआ था, तो हर chromosome Meiosis two में पहले से duplicated घुसता है। ये भी साफ़ सही है।
Step three, और असल में mark यहीं है। क्या R, A को explain करता है? दो trues इसे तय नहीं करते — आपको पूछना होगा कि क्या दूसरा वाक्य पहले की वजह है, या बस पास खड़ा एक सच।

और जवाब है हाँ, सीधे। चूँकि duplicated chromatids पहले से मौजूद हैं और उन्हें सिर्फ़ separate होना है, कोई और replication ज़रूरी नहीं। R, A के पास खड़ा कोई इत्तेफ़ाक़ नहीं — R वजह है कि A सच है। दरअसल, दोबारा replicate करना reduction को पूरी तरह बर्बाद कर देता।

तो जवाब है A — दोनों सच, और R correct explanation है। इसे पिछले part वाले assertion reason से मिलाइए, जहाँ जवाब था A सच, R झूठा। वही तीन step वाला तरीक़ा, अलग फ़ैसला। तरीक़ा आप साथ रखते हैं; फ़ैसला हर बार बदलता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls 1 and 2 — the phantom S phase, and the two anaphases

board_events.text: Pitfall 1: assuming DNA replicates before Meiosis II
It does NOT. Interkinesis has no S phase. The chromosomes are already duplicated from before Meiosis I.
The name is doing the damage — 'interkinesis' sounds like an interphase, so students fill in an S phase that is not there.
Pitfall 2: mixing up what separates in anaphase I versus anaphase II
Anaphase I = HOMOLOGOUS CHROMOSOMES. Anaphase II = SISTER CHROMATIDS.
This pair is the most examined distinction in the chapter.
Derive it rather than recall it: Meiosis I must halve, and only separating a PAIR can halve.

segments.text: Two pitfalls here, and the first is the defining error of this subtopic.
It does not. Interkinesis has no S phase. The chromosomes are already duplicated from before Meiosis one. Say it flatly, because there is no nuance to add.

I think the name is what does the damage. Interkinesis sounds like interphase, and interphase is where S phase lives, so students hear a stage between two divisions and fill in a replication that is not there. Recognise that pull and resist it.
Pitfall two is the most examined distinction in the entire chapter, so it earns its own repetition.
Anaphase one separates homologous chromosomes. Anaphase two separates sister chromatids. Two lines. If you can produce those two lines on demand you have a large share of this chapter's marks.

And the reason it is examined so relentlessly is that both statements are true of one anaphase each — so a distractor is never obviously absurd. It is always half right, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.

So derive it instead of recalling it. Meiosis one must halve the number. And the only way to halve a count is to separate a pair — splitting one chromosome's own chromatids cannot halve anything. So anaphase one must be separating homologues. The logic reconstructs the fact.
यहाँ दो pitfalls, और पहला इस subtopic की सबसे ख़ास ग़लती है।
नहीं होता। Interkinesis में कोई S phase नहीं। Chromosomes पहले से duplicated हैं, Meiosis one से भी पहले से। इसे सपाट कहिए, क्योंकि इसमें जोड़ने को कोई बारीकी है ही नहीं।

मुझे लगता है नुक़सान नाम ही करता है। Interkinesis, interphase जैसा सुनाई देता है, और S phase interphase में ही रहता है, तो students दो divisions के बीच एक stage सुनते हैं और वहाँ एक replication भर देते हैं जो है ही नहीं। इस खिंचाव को पहचानिए और रोकिए।
Pitfall दो पूरे chapter की सबसे ज़्यादा जाँची जाने वाली distinction है, तो इसका दोहराया जाना बनता है।
Anaphase one, homologous chromosomes को separate करता है। Anaphase two, sister chromatids को। दो lines. अगर आप ये दो lines माँगने पर बोल सकें, तो इस chapter के बहुत सारे marks आपके हैं।

और इसे इतनी बेरहमी से इसलिए पूछा जाता है क्योंकि दोनों statements किसी ना किसी anaphase के लिए सच हैं — तो distractor कभी साफ़-साफ़ बेतुका नहीं होता। वो हमेशा आधा सही होता है, और यही उसे ख़तरनाक बनाता है।

तो याद करने की जगह derive कीजिए। Meiosis one को number आधा करना ही है। और count को आधा करने का इकलौता तरीक़ा है एक जोड़ी को अलग करना — एक chromosome के अपने chromatids को तोड़ने से कुछ आधा नहीं होता। तो anaphase one को homologues ही अलग करने होंगे। Logic ख़ुद fact दोबारा बना देता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls 3 and 4 — 'same as mitosis', and what gets halved

board_events.text: Pitfall 3: calling Meiosis II 'the same as mitosis'
Both are equational — that much is true. But Meiosis II begins with HAPLOID cells and is NEVER preceded by replication.
The assertion 'Meiosis II resembles mitosis' is TRUE. It is the reason attached to it that is usually false.
Pitfall 4: thinking only the chromosome number is halved
After Meiosis II, BOTH the chromosome number AND the DNA amount are reduced to half of the diploid parent.
The chromatids that carried the duplicate DNA were parcelled out into separate cells.
Track chromosome number and DNA amount as SEPARATE quantities. They halve at different moments.

segments.text: Two more pitfalls, and both are cases of a true statement being stretched one step too far.

Both are equational, and that much is genuinely true. But Meiosis two begins with haploid cells, and it is never preceded by replication. Mitosis can begin with diploid or haploid cells, and it is always preceded by an S phase.

This is worth flagging as a question pattern. The assertion Meiosis two resembles mitosis is true, and the paper knows it is true. What it does is attach a false reason — for example, that both separate homologous chromosomes. They do not; both separate chromatids. A true assertion with a false reason gives option C.
Pitfall four is a counting error, and it is the one that separates the top scorers on this chapter.
After Meiosis two, both the chromosome number and the D N A amount are reduced to half of the diploid parent. Both. Not just the number.

And the reason is mechanical rather than mysterious. The chromatids that carried the duplicate D N A were parcelled out into separate cells. If the D N A leaves in a chromatid, and the chromatid goes to another cell, then the D N A went with it.

So track them as separate quantities, because they halve at different moments. The chromosome number halved once, at anaphase one. The D N A amount halved twice — once at each division. Same process, two different schedules.
दो और pitfalls, और दोनों ऐसे मामले हैं जहाँ एक सच्ची बात को एक क़दम ज़्यादा खींच दिया गया है।

दोनों equational हैं, और इतना सचमुच सही है। पर Meiosis two haploid cells से शुरू होता है, और उससे पहले कभी replication नहीं होता। Mitosis diploid या haploid से शुरू हो सकता है, और उससे पहले हमेशा एक S phase होता है।

इसे एक question pattern की तरह flag करना ज़रूरी है। Assertion कि Meiosis two, mitosis जैसा है — ये सच है, और paper जानता है कि सच है। वो करता ये है कि उसके साथ एक झूठा reason जोड़ देता है — मसलन, कि दोनों homologous chromosomes को separate करते हैं। नहीं करते; दोनों chromatids को करते हैं। सच्चा assertion और झूठा reason मिलकर option C देते हैं।
Pitfall चार एक counting की ग़लती है, और यही इस chapter में top scorers को अलग करती है।
Meiosis two के बाद, chromosome number और D N A amount, दोनों diploid parent के आधे रह जाते हैं। दोनों। सिर्फ़ number नहीं।

और वजह रहस्यमय नहीं, mechanical है। जो chromatids duplicate D N A लिए थे वो अलग-अलग cells में बँट गए। अगर D N A किसी chromatid में जाता है, और वो chromatid दूसरे cell में जाता है, तो D N A उसके साथ चला गया।

तो इन्हें अलग quantities की तरह track कीजिए, क्योंकि ये अलग पलों पर आधे होते हैं। Chromosome number एक बार आधा हुआ, anaphase one पर। D N A amount दो बार आधी हुई — हर division पर एक बार। वही process, दो अलग schedules.

sections.title: Pro-tips: divide by four, and 'reduce, then split'

board_events.text: Pro-Tip 1: for any counting problem, anchor on one meiosis $\to$ four haploid cells
One meiosis $\to$ FOUR haploid cells (for spores and pollen). So: meiocytes needed = cells required $\div$ 4.
Do not confuse this with the mitotic rule. Mitosis compounds as $2^n$; meiosis is a fixed one-off giving 4.
Pro-Tip 2: for stage-counting, remember the rhythm 'reduce, then split'
Meiosis I REDUCES the number. Meiosis II SPLITS the chromatids.
From that rhythm you can rebuild: what separates, which is reductional, and what the counts are at every stage.
Derived knowledge survives exam pressure. Memorised lists do not.

segments.text: We close this part with two pro tips — one for the numericals, one for the concepts.

For any how many divisions or how many cells problem in meiosis, anchor on one meiosis giving four haploid cells — for spores and pollen. So meiocytes needed equals cells required divided by four. One rule, one division sum.

And do not confuse this with the mitotic rule from part one. Mitosis repeats, so its count compounds as two to the power n. Meiosis does not repeat — it is a fixed, one off process that yields exactly four. Two rules, two processes. Check which one the question is about before you reach.
And the second pro tip, which is the one to carry into every conceptual question in this chapter.

Reduce, then split. Meiosis one reduces the number. Meiosis two splits the chromatids. Three words, and they order the entire process — which division comes first, what each one does, and which label each one carries.

And notice how much you can rebuild from those three words. What separates in each anaphase — reduce means homologues, split means chromatids. Which division is reductional — the one that reduces. What the counts are at every stage. You are not memorising four facts; you are deriving them from one phrase.

<excited>And that is really the lesson of this whole chapter. Derived knowledge survives exam pressure; memorised lists do not. When you are three hours in and tired, you will not reliably recall a list of four labels — but you will recall reduce, then split, and everything else falls out of it.
हम इस part को दो pro tips के साथ बंद करते हैं — एक numericals के लिए, एक concepts के लिए।

Meiosis में कोई भी how many divisions या how many cells वाली problem हो, इस पर anchor कीजिए कि एक meiosis चार haploid cells देता है — spores और pollen के लिए। तो meiocytes चाहिए बराबर cells required divided by four. एक rule, एक भाग का सवाल।

और इसे part one वाले mitotic rule से मत मिलाइए। Mitosis दोहराता है, तो उसका count two to the power n की तरह compound होता है। Meiosis दोहराता नहीं — वो एक तय, एक-बारगी process है जो ठीक चार देता है। दो rules, दो processes. हाथ बढ़ाने से पहले देखिए सवाल किस बारे में है।
और दूसरी pro tip, जो इस chapter के हर conceptual सवाल में साथ ले जाने लायक़ है।

Reduce, then split. Meiosis one number को reduce करता है। Meiosis two chromatids को split करता है। तीन शब्द, और वो पूरे process को क्रम में रख देते हैं — कौन सा division पहले आता है, हर एक क्या करता है, और हर एक पर कौन सा label लगता है।

और ग़ौर कीजिए उन तीन शब्दों से आप कितना दोबारा बना सकते हैं। हर anaphase में क्या separate होता है — reduce मतलब homologues, split मतलब chromatids. कौन सा division reductional है — जो reduce करता है। हर stage पर counts क्या हैं। आप चार facts रट नहीं रहे; आप उन्हें एक वाक्यांश से derive कर रहे हैं।

<excited>और यही असल में इस पूरे chapter का सबक़ है। Derived knowledge exam के दबाव में टिकती है; रटी हुई lists नहीं। जब आप तीन घंटे बाद थके हुए होंगे, तो चार labels की list भरोसे से याद नहीं आएगी — पर reduce, then split याद आ जाएगा, और बाक़ी सब उसी से निकल आएगा।

board_events.text: Is the cell part of the body's GROWTH and MAINTENANCE — or part of making the NEXT GENERATION?
Growth and maintenance $\Rightarrow$ MITOSIS. Making the next generation $\Rightarrow$ MEIOSIS.
This life-cycle framing underpins how every cell-division question is set.
This part is the integration that ties the whole chapter together.
'Differentiate mitosis from meiosis' is one of the most reliably asked questions across CBSE Boards and NEET.

segments.text: <curious>We have spent three parts inside the machinery. Now let us climb out and ask the question that decides everything before any of that machinery starts turning.
A cell never divides at random. We opened this chapter with that idea and now we can complete it. The kind of division a cell performs depends entirely on what that cell is and what its role is.
And really it comes down to a single question with two answers. What is this cell for? Everything branches from there.
Ask it precisely. Is the cell part of the body's growth and maintenance? Or is it part of making the next generation? Those are the only two answers, and each one selects a division.
Growth and maintenance means mitosis. Making the next generation means meiosis. That is the whole decision, and notice it is a question about purpose, not about mechanism.

And this framing is worth more than it looks. The haploid diploid life cycle framing underpins how every cell division question is set. Once you see where a cell sits in the life cycle, the rest of the answer usually follows without any further recall.

So treat this part as the integration. We are not learning new stages. We are connecting the ones you already know into one picture, and then compressing that picture into something you can carry into an exam hall.

And there is a very practical reason to take it seriously. Differentiate mitosis from meiosis is one of the most reliably asked questions across C B S E Boards, worth three to five marks, and it appears in NEET as match the column or pick the difference. This is not optional revision.
<curious>हमने तीन parts machinery के अंदर बिताए। अब बाहर निकलकर वो सवाल पूछते हैं जो उस machinery के चलने से भी पहले सब कुछ तय कर देता है।

Cell कभी बेतरतीब divide नहीं करता। हमने इस chapter की शुरुआत इसी idea से की थी और अब उसे पूरा कर सकते हैं। कोई cell किस क़िस्म का division करेगा, ये पूरी तरह इस पर निर्भर है कि वो cell क्या है और उसका role क्या है।
और असल में ये एक ही सवाल पर आ टिकता है, जिसके दो जवाब हैं। ये cell किस लिए है? सब कुछ वहीं से बँट जाता है।
इसे precisely पूछिए। क्या ये cell शरीर की growth और maintenance का हिस्सा है? या अगली generation बनाने का हिस्सा? यही दो जवाब हैं, और हर एक एक division चुन लेता है।
Growth और maintenance मतलब mitosis. अगली generation बनाना मतलब meiosis. यही पूरा फ़ैसला है, और ग़ौर कीजिए ये सवाल मक़सद का है, mechanism का नहीं।

और ये framing दिखने से ज़्यादा क़ीमती है। Haploid diploid life cycle वाली framing तय करती है कि cell division का हर सवाल कैसे बनाया जाता है। एक बार आप देख लें कि cell life cycle में कहाँ बैठा है, बाक़ी जवाब अक्सर बिना और कुछ याद किए निकल आता है।
तो इस part को integration समझिए। हम नए stages नहीं सीख रहे। हम उन्हें जोड़ रहे हैं जो आपको पहले से आते हैं, एक तस्वीर में — और फिर उस तस्वीर को कुछ ऐसा बना रहे हैं जिसे आप exam hall में ले जा सकें।

और इसे गंभीरता से लेने की एक बहुत practical वजह है। Differentiate mitosis from meiosis, C B S E Boards में सबसे भरोसे से पूछे जाने वाले सवालों में है, तीन से पाँच marks का, और N E E T में ये match the column या pick the difference की शक्ल में आता है। ये optional revision नहीं है।

board_events.text: Mitosis runs in the body's SOMATIC (diploid) cells.
And in the MERISTEMATIC tissues of plants — the apical and lateral meristems.
Its job: GROWTH, REPAIR and REPLACEMENT.
It produces genetically identical diploid cells — so the body stays ONE consistent genome.
Remember the caveat from Part 1: mitosis is TYPICALLY somatic and diploid — but it also runs in haploid cells.
So 'somatic and diploid' is where mitosis usually happens — not a restriction on where it can.

segments.text: Take the first branch. Where in an organism does mitosis actually happen? There are two answers worth naming, and one caveat worth remembering.
Two territories on the top row, the job underneath, and the caveat in red at the bottom.
Mitosis runs in the body's somatic cells, which are diploid. Somatic simply means of the body — as opposed to the germ line. So essentially everything you are made of divides this way.

And in plants there is a specific address worth naming. The meristematic tissues — the apical and lateral meristems. Apical at the growing tips, lateral for thickening. Name both if a question asks where mitosis occurs in a plant.

Its job is growth, repair and replacement. Three words. And you met all three back in part one when we did the significance of mitosis — this is the same content, now located in the body rather than described in the abstract.

And here is the reason it must be equational. Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid cells, so the body stays one consistent genome. Every cell in you carries the same instructions. That consistency is not a nice extra — it is what lets tissues work together at all.

But hold on to the caveat from part one, because a capstone summary is exactly where over-generalising becomes tempting. Mitosis is typically somatic and diploid — but it also runs in haploid cells. The honeybee drone is our example.

So read it as a description, not a restriction. Somatic and diploid is where mitosis usually happens, not a rule about where it can happen. And that distinction matters, because meiosis — as we are about to see — really does have a hard restriction.
पहली शाखा लीजिए। किसी organism में mitosis असल में कहाँ होता है? दो जवाब नाम लेने लायक़ हैं, और एक caveat याद रखने लायक़।
ऊपर की row में दो territories, नीचे काम, और सबसे नीचे लाल रंग में caveat.
Mitosis शरीर के somatic cells में चलता है, जो diploid हैं। Somatic का मतलब बस शरीर का — germ line के उलट। तो आप जिस चीज़ से बने हैं, वो लगभग सब इसी तरह divide करती है।

और plants में एक ख़ास पता है जो नाम लेने लायक़ है। Meristematic tissues — apical और lateral meristems. Apical बढ़ते सिरों पर, lateral मोटाई के लिए। अगर सवाल पूछे plant में mitosis कहाँ होता है, तो दोनों का नाम लीजिए।

उसका काम है growth, repair और replacement. तीन शब्द। और आप तीनों से part one में मिल चुके हैं जब हमने mitosis की significance की थी — यही content है, अब abstract में बताया नहीं, शरीर में जगह देकर रखा गया है।

और यही वजह है कि उसे equational होना ही है। Mitosis genetically identical diploid cells बनाता है, ताकि शरीर एक consistent genome बना रहे। आपका हर cell वही instructions रखता है। ये consistency कोई सुंदर बोनस नहीं — यही tissues को साथ काम करने देती है।

पर part one वाला caveat पकड़े रहिए, क्योंकि capstone summary ही वो जगह है जहाँ ज़्यादा generalise करने का लालच आता है। Mitosis आमतौर पर somatic और diploid है — पर वो haploid cells में भी चलता है। Honeybee drone हमारा example है।

तो इसे description की तरह पढ़िए, restriction की तरह नहीं। Somatic और diploid वो जगह है जहाँ mitosis आमतौर पर होता है, ये नियम नहीं कि वो कहाँ हो सकता है। और ये फ़र्क़ मायने रखता है, क्योंकि meiosis पर — जैसा हम अभी देखेंगे — सचमुच एक सख़्त पाबंदी है।

board_events.text: Meiocytes are also called the GAMETE MOTHER CELLS, or the GERM-LINE cells.
Its job: to make HAPLOID gametes or spores.
It halves the chromosome number so that the next generation does NOT double at fertilisation.
Why ONLY diploid? Because synapsis needs homologous PAIRS — and a haploid cell has no partner to pair with.
And note the second half of the scope: only diploid cells, and only ONCE in the life cycle.

segments.text: Now the other branch, and here the language is much more restrictive. Notice the word only is about to do a lot of work.
Meiosis runs only in specialised diploid cells called meiocytes. Only. That is a genuine restriction, unlike mitosis's typically, and it is enforced by the biology rather than just being usual.
The meiocyte on the left, its aliases beside it, and underneath the reason the whole restriction exists.

Meiocytes go by other names, and a question may use any of them. Gamete mother cells. Germ line cells. And we met a specific one in part three — the pollen mother cell of a plant. All the same category.
Its job is to make haploid gametes or spores. Note it is gametes or spores, not just gametes — plants make spores by meiosis too, and a question about a plant will often say spore.

And the purpose behind it. Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that the next generation does not double its chromosomes at fertilisation. That is the argument we built in part three, and it is the reason the restriction exists at all.

So why only diploid cells? Trace it back. Synapsis is the central event of prophase one, and synapsis needs homologous pairs. A haploid cell has one of each chromosome, so there is no partner in the room. The restriction is not a rule to memorise — it is a consequence.

And note the second half of the scope, which is easy to drop. Only diploid cells, and only once in the life cycle. Mitosis runs again and again throughout a lifetime; meiosis is a single scheduled event at one specific point.
अब दूसरी शाखा, और यहाँ भाषा कहीं ज़्यादा सख़्त है। ग़ौर कीजिए only शब्द बहुत काम करने वाला है।
Meiosis सिर्फ़ specialised diploid cells में चलता है जिन्हें meiocytes कहते हैं। सिर्फ़। ये एक असली पाबंदी है, mitosis के typically के उलट, और इसे biology लागू करती है — ये बस आम बात नहीं है।
बाईं तरफ़ meiocyte, उसके साथ उसके दूसरे नाम, और नीचे वो वजह जिससे ये पूरी पाबंदी मौजूद है।
Meiocytes के दूसरे नाम भी हैं, और सवाल कोई भी इस्तेमाल कर सकता है। Gamete mother cells. Germ line cells. और part three में हम एक ख़ास से मिले थे — plant का pollen mother cell. सब एक ही श्रेणी।
उसका काम है haploid gametes या spores बनाना। ग़ौर कीजिए gametes या spores, सिर्फ़ gametes नहीं — plants भी meiosis से spores बनाते हैं, और plant वाला सवाल अक्सर spore कहेगा।

और इसके पीछे का मक़सद। Meiosis chromosome number को आधा करता है ताकि अगली generation fertilisation पर अपने chromosomes double ना कर ले। यही वो दलील है जो हमने part three में बनाई थी, और यही वजह है कि ये पाबंदी है ही।

तो सिर्फ़ diploid cells ही क्यों? पीछे जाइए। Synapsis prophase one का central event है, और synapsis को homologous pairs चाहिए। Haploid cell में हर chromosome का एक ही है, तो कमरे में कोई partner नहीं। ये पाबंदी रटने का नियम नहीं — ये एक नतीजा है।

और scope का दूसरा आधा हिस्सा भी देखिए, जो छूट जाना आसान है। सिर्फ़ diploid cells, और life cycle में सिर्फ़ एक बार। Mitosis पूरी ज़िंदगी बार-बार चलता है; meiosis एक ही scheduled event है, एक ख़ास मौक़े पर।

board_events.text: A haploid male gamete (n) fuses with a haploid female gamete (n) to restore the diploid (2n) zygote.
The zygote then grows by MITOSIS into a new diploid body.
So a sexually reproducing organism ALTERNATES between two phases.
The DIPLOID phase — the body, built by mitosis. The HAPLOID phase — the gametes, made by meiosis.
Fertilisation doubles. That is not optional — it is what fertilisation IS.
Meiosis and fertilisation are two halves of one accounting system.

segments.text: We now have two divisions running in two different territories. What connects them? A third event, which is not a division at all.
Follow the row. Male gamete n, plus female gamete n, fusing at fertilisation into a two n zygote, which then grows by mitosis into a new diploid body.

A haploid male gamete fuses with a haploid female gamete to restore the diploid zygote. n plus n gives two n. Fertilisation is a doubling event — it is the only thing in this chapter that increases the chromosome number.
And the zygote then grows by mitosis into a new diploid body. Which closes the circle — that new body will eventually make meiocytes of its own, and the whole thing runs again.

So a sexually reproducing organism alternates between two phases. That word alternates is doing real work — it is not that an organism is diploid and occasionally makes haploid cells. It genuinely passes through both states.

The diploid phase is the body, built by mitosis. The haploid phase is the gametes, made by meiosis. Two phases, each with its own division. Learn the pairing, because a question can hand you either half and ask for the other.

And here is the point that makes meiosis necessary rather than merely useful. Fertilisation doubles. That is not optional; that is what fertilisation is. Two cells fusing into one. So something must pay that doubling back before the next fertilisation, and only meiosis can.

So do not think of them as separate topics. Meiosis and fertilisation are two halves of one accounting system — one debits, one credits, and the books balance across a generation. That is the frame the next section makes explicit.
अब हमारे पास दो divisions हैं जो दो अलग territories में चल रहे हैं। इन्हें जोड़ता क्या है? एक तीसरा event, जो division है ही नहीं।
Row follow कीजिए। Male gamete n, plus female gamete n, fertilisation पर मिलकर two n zygote बनते हैं, जो फिर mitosis से बढ़कर एक नया diploid body बन जाता है।

एक haploid male gamete, एक haploid female gamete से मिलकर diploid zygote बहाल कर देता है। n plus n यानी two n. Fertilisation एक doubling event है — इस chapter में यही अकेली चीज़ है जो chromosome number बढ़ाती है।
और फिर zygote mitosis से बढ़कर एक नया diploid body बन जाता है। जिससे घेरा बंद हो जाता है — वो नया शरीर आगे चलकर अपने meiocytes बनाएगा, और पूरी चीज़ दोबारा चलेगी।

तो एक sexually reproducing organism दो phases के बीच alternate करता है। Alternates शब्द असली काम कर रहा है — ऐसा नहीं कि organism diploid है और कभी-कभार haploid cells बना लेता है। वो सचमुच दोनों हालतों से गुज़रता है।
Diploid phase शरीर है, mitosis से बना। Haploid phase gametes हैं, meiosis से बने। दो phases, हर एक का अपना division. जोड़ी सीखिए, क्योंकि सवाल आपको कोई भी आधा हिस्सा देकर दूसरा माँग सकता है।

और यहाँ वो बात है जो meiosis को सिर्फ़ उपयोगी नहीं, ज़रूरी बना देती है। Fertilisation double करता है। ये optional नहीं; fertilisation है ही यही। दो cells मिलकर एक। तो अगले fertilisation से पहले किसी को वो doubling चुकानी होगी, और सिर्फ़ meiosis चुका सकता है।

तो इन्हें अलग topics मत समझिए। Meiosis और fertilisation एक ही accounting system के दो आधे हिस्से हैं — एक debit करता है, एक credit, और एक generation के आर-पार खाता बराबर हो जाता है। अगला section इसी frame को साफ़ करता है।

board_events.text: Note the two halves of the circle: the DIPLOID phase and the HAPLOID phase.
MEIOSIS HALVES. FERTILISATION RESTORES. MITOSIS MULTIPLIES.
Each clause names one arrow on the circle, and each does a job the other two cannot.
Keep this in mind and no counting question can trip you up.
Every stage you have learned in this chapter sits somewhere on this circle.

segments.text: <excited>Everything in this chapter now collapses into one circle and one sentence. If you remember nothing else from this part, remember what is on this diagram.

Trace the circle. Top, the diploid adult body at two n. Meiosis in its meiocytes takes it down to haploid gametes at n. Two gametes fuse at fertilisation, back to a two n zygote. And mitosis grows the zygote back into the adult body. One loop, three arrows.

And notice the circle is shaded in two halves. The diploid phase occupies one half, the haploid phase the other. An organism's entire existence is a journey around this loop, spending most of it in one half.
And here is the master logic, in three clauses. Meiosis halves. Fertilisation restores. Mitosis multiplies. Say it out loud once. Meiosis halves, fertilisation restores, mitosis multiplies.

Each clause names one arrow on the circle, and each does a job the other two cannot. Meiosis is the only thing that reduces. Fertilisation is the only thing that increases. Mitosis is the only thing that amplifies without changing anything.

Keep this in mind and no counting question can trip you up. That is a strong claim, so let me justify it. Every counting question in this chapter is asking where on this circle a cell sits, and what the next arrow does to it. Locate the cell, name the arrow, and the number follows.

And that is the integration. Every stage you have learned — G one, S phase, P M A T, the five sub-stages of prophase one, interkinesis, all of it — sits somewhere on this circle. You have not been learning a list of stages. You have been learning one loop, in detail.
<excited>इस chapter का सब कुछ अब एक घेरे और एक वाक्य में सिमट जाता है। अगर इस part से आपको और कुछ याद ना रहे, तो इस diagram पर जो है वो याद रखिए।

घेरे को trace कीजिए। ऊपर, two n पर diploid adult body. उसके meiocytes में meiosis उसे नीचे haploid gametes तक, n पर लाता है। दो gametes fertilisation पर मिलते हैं, वापस two n zygote पर। और mitosis zygote को वापस adult body बना देता है। एक loop, तीन arrows.
और ग़ौर कीजिए घेरा दो हिस्सों में रंगा है। एक आधे में diploid phase, दूसरे में haploid. किसी organism का पूरा वजूद इसी loop का सफ़र है, जिसका ज़्यादातर हिस्सा एक ही आधे में बीतता है।
और यहाँ है master logic, तीन हिस्सों में। Meiosis halves. Fertilisation restores. Mitosis multiplies. एक बार ज़ोर से बोलिए। Meiosis halves, fertilisation restores, mitosis multiplies.
हर हिस्सा घेरे के एक arrow का नाम लेता है, और हर एक वो काम करता है जो बाक़ी दो नहीं कर सकते। सिर्फ़ meiosis घटाता है। सिर्फ़ fertilisation बढ़ाता है। सिर्फ़ mitosis बिना कुछ बदले बढ़ाता है।

इसे याद रखिए और कोई counting सवाल आपको नहीं गिरा सकता। ये बड़ा दावा है, तो इसे साबित करता हूँ। इस chapter का हर counting सवाल यही पूछ रहा है कि cell इस घेरे पर कहाँ बैठा है, और अगला arrow उसके साथ क्या करता है। Cell को ढूँढिए, arrow का नाम लीजिए, और number अपने आप निकल आएगा।

और यही integration है। आपने जो भी stage सीखा — G one, S phase, P M A T, prophase one के पाँच sub-stages, interkinesis, सब — इसी घेरे पर कहीं बैठा है। आप stages की list नहीं सीख रहे थे। आप एक loop सीख रहे थे, बारीकी से।

board_events.text: Number of divisions — MITOSIS: one. MEIOSIS: two (Meiosis I + Meiosis II).
Rounds of DNA replication — MITOSIS: one (before the single division). MEIOSIS: one (before Meiosis I only; NONE before Meiosis II).
Note the asymmetry: this is the only row where meiosis has FEWER of something than you would expect.
That single asymmetry — two divisions, one replication — is what produces the halving.
Type of cell — MITOSIS: somatic cells, both haploid and diploid. MEIOSIS: only diploid cells (meiocytes).
Learn this table as a UNIT — not as twelve unrelated facts.

segments.text: Now the table that is the heart of differentiate questions. It has twelve rows, which is too many to swallow at once, so we will take it in four bites of three. This first bite is the architecture.
Three rows. Number of divisions, rounds of D N A replication, and the type of cell it occurs in.
Number of divisions. Mitosis, one. Meiosis, two — Meiosis one plus Meiosis two. Simple, and it is the row everything else hangs from.

Rounds of D N A replication. Mitosis, one, before its single division. Meiosis, also one — before Meiosis one only, and none before Meiosis two. Read that carefully, because it is the strangest row in the table.

And notice the asymmetry, because it is the whole trick of meiosis. Every other row gives meiosis more than mitosis — more divisions, more daughters, more events. This is the only row where meiosis has fewer of something than you would expect. Two divisions, but still only one replication.

And that single asymmetry is what produces the halving. Two divisions off one replication. If meiosis replicated before each division, like mitosis does, it would end with four diploid cells and reduce nothing at all.
Type of cell it occurs in. Mitosis, somatic cells, both haploid and diploid. Meiosis, only diploid cells — meiocytes. There is the both versus only contrast again, and we have already traced why.

One instruction before we go on. Learn this table as a unit, not as twelve unrelated facts. Rows connect to each other, as row two and row one just did. When a row surprises you, ask which other row explains it.
अब वो table जो differentiate वाले सवालों का दिल है। इसमें बारह rows हैं, जो एक बार में निगलने के लिए बहुत हैं, तो हम इसे तीन-तीन के चार टुकड़ों में लेंगे। ये पहला टुकड़ा architecture है।
तीन rows. कितने divisions, D N A replication के कितने rounds, और किस क़िस्म के cell में होता है।
कितने divisions. Mitosis, एक। Meiosis, दो — Meiosis one plus Meiosis two. आसान, और यही वो row है जिससे बाक़ी सब टँगा है।

D N A replication के rounds. Mitosis, एक, उसके इकलौते division से पहले। Meiosis, भी एक — सिर्फ़ Meiosis one से पहले, और Meiosis two से पहले कोई नहीं। इसे ध्यान से पढ़िए, क्योंकि ये table की सबसे अजीब row है।

और asymmetry पर ग़ौर कीजिए, क्योंकि meiosis की पूरी चाल यही है। बाक़ी हर row meiosis को mitosis से ज़्यादा देती है — ज़्यादा divisions, ज़्यादा daughters, ज़्यादा events. सिर्फ़ यही row है जहाँ meiosis के पास आपकी उम्मीद से कम है। दो divisions, पर replication फिर भी एक ही।

और यही एक asymmetry halving पैदा करती है। एक replication पर दो divisions. अगर meiosis हर division से पहले replicate करता, mitosis की तरह, तो वो चार diploid cells पर ख़त्म होता और कुछ reduce ही ना करता।
किस क़िस्म के cell में होता है। Mitosis, somatic cells, haploid और diploid दोनों। Meiosis, सिर्फ़ diploid cells — meiocytes. वही both बनाम only वाला contrast फिर से, और हम वजह ढूँढ चुके हैं।

आगे बढ़ने से पहले एक हिदायत। इस table को एक unit की तरह सीखिए, बारह अलग-अलग facts की तरह नहीं। Rows आपस में जुड़ी हैं, जैसे अभी row दो और row एक जुड़ीं। जब कोई row चौंकाए, तो पूछिए कौन सी दूसरी row उसे समझाती है।

<text x="130" y="146" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">recombination</text>
<text x="350" y="136" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Does NOT occur</text>
<text x="540" y="136" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">Occurs in Pachytene of Meiosis I</text>

<text x="350" y="178" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Two</text>
<text x="540" y="178" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#d97706">Four</text>
<line x1="244" y1="36" x2="244" y2="194" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-width="1"/>
<line x1="456" y1="36" x2="456" y2="194" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-width="1"/>

<text x="330" y="218" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">The first two rows are the ONLY-IN-MEIOSIS rows. Any question mentioning synapsis or crossing over has already told you the answer.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Pairing of homologues — MITOSIS: does not occur. MEIOSIS: occurs in Prophase I (synapsis).
Crossing over / recombination — MITOSIS: does not occur. MEIOSIS: occurs in Pachytene of Meiosis I.
These two are the ONLY-IN-MEIOSIS rows. Any question mentioning synapsis or crossing over has already told you the answer.
Daughter cells produced — MITOSIS: two. MEIOSIS: four.
Notice how row 6 falls straight out of row 1. Two divisions instead of one gives twice as many products.
Two divisions, one replication, four daughters, half the number. Four facts, one cause.

segments.text: Second bite, and these three rows are the most useful in the whole table — because two of them are pure give-aways.
Look at the first two rows and notice they have the same shape. Does not occur, versus occurs — with a stage attached.

Pairing of homologues. Mitosis, does not occur. Meiosis, occurs in prophase one, and it is called synapsis. Note the answer gives the stage, not just a yes — an exam answer should always name prophase one here.
Crossing over, also called recombination. Mitosis, does not occur. Meiosis, occurs in pachytene of Meiosis one. Again, name the sub-stage. Pachytene, not just prophase one.

<excited>And here is why these two rows are worth more than the other ten. These are the only in meiosis rows. Any question that mentions synapsis, or crossing over, or bivalents, or chiasmata has already told you the answer before you have finished reading it. Those words cannot appear in mitosis.
Daughter cells produced. Mitosis, two. Meiosis, four. And that follows directly from row one — two divisions instead of one, so twice as many products.

So the table is already rewarding you for learning it as a unit. Row six is not a new fact — it is row one, restated as an outcome. Every time you can derive a row from another row, that is one fewer thing to memorise.

In fact, put four of the rows together and they are all one cause. Two divisions, one replication, four daughters, half the chromosome number. Those are not four facts — they are one architectural decision, seen from four angles.
दूसरा टुकड़ा, और ये तीन rows पूरी table में सबसे काम की हैं — क्योंकि इनमें से दो तो सीधे जवाब दे देती हैं।
पहली दो rows देखिए और ग़ौर कीजिए उनका shape एक जैसा है। Does not occur, बनाम occurs — और साथ में एक stage.

Homologues का pairing. Mitosis, नहीं होता। Meiosis, prophase one में होता है, और उसे synapsis कहते हैं। ग़ौर कीजिए जवाब stage देता है, सिर्फ़ हाँ नहीं — exam के जवाब में हमेशा prophase one का नाम लीजिए।
Crossing over, जिसे recombination भी कहते हैं। Mitosis, नहीं होता। Meiosis, Meiosis one के pachytene में होता है। फिर से, sub-stage का नाम लीजिए। Pachytene, सिर्फ़ prophase one नहीं।

<excited>और यही वजह है कि ये दो rows बाक़ी दस से ज़्यादा क़ीमती हैं। ये only in meiosis वाली rows हैं। जो भी सवाल synapsis, या crossing over, या bivalents, या chiasmata का ज़िक्र करे, वो आपका पढ़ना ख़त्म होने से पहले ही जवाब दे चुका है। ये शब्द mitosis में आ ही नहीं सकते।
कितने daughter cells बनते हैं। Mitosis, दो। Meiosis, चार। और ये सीधे row one से निकलता है — एक की जगह दो divisions, तो दोगुने products.
तो table आपको unit की तरह सीखने का इनाम अभी से दे रही है। Row six कोई नया fact नहीं — वो row one ही है, नतीजे की शक्ल में। जब भी आप किसी row को दूसरी row से derive कर सकें, वो एक चीज़ कम रटने को।
दरअसल, चार rows को साथ रखिए और वो सब एक ही वजह हैं। दो divisions, एक replication, चार daughters, आधा chromosome number. ये चार facts नहीं — ये एक ही architectural फ़ैसला है, चार कोणों से देखा हुआ।

board_events.text: Chromosome number of daughters — MITOSIS: same as parent ($2n \to 2n$). MEIOSIS: half of parent ($2n \to n$).
Genetic make-up of daughters — MITOSIS: identical to parent. MEIOSIS: genetically distinct (varied).
What separates in the key anaphase — MITOSIS: sister chromatids. MEIOSIS: HOMOLOGUES in Anaphase I; sister chromatids in Anaphase II.
This row is the single most examined line in the entire chapter.
And notice row 9 CAUSES row 7. Separating a pair halves the count; separating chromatids does not.
So if you can only remember one row, remember row 9 — and derive row 7 from it.

segments.text: Third bite. These three rows describe the outcome — what the daughter cells actually walk away with. And the last of them is the most examined line in the entire chapter.
Three rows. Chromosome number of the daughters, their genetic make up, and what separates in the key anaphase.

Chromosome number of the daughters. Mitosis, same as parent — two n to two n. Meiosis, half of parent — two n to n. This is the equational versus reductional distinction, stated as an outcome instead of a label.

Genetic make up of the daughters. Mitosis, identical to parent. Meiosis, genetically distinct — varied. And notice these are two independent claims. Mitosis matches the parent in both number and content; meiosis differs in both.

What separates in the key anaphase. Mitosis, sister chromatids. Meiosis — and this is a two part answer — homologues in anaphase one, sister chromatids in anaphase two. Give both halves. An answer that just says homologues is only half right.
This row is the single most examined line in the entire chapter. We have flagged it in every part, and here it is one last time. If you are short on revision time, this is the row to know cold.

And notice the causal link, because it means you only need one of these rows. Row nine causes row seven. Separating a pair halves the count. Separating a chromosome's own chromatids does not. So what separates determines what the daughters get.
So if you can only remember one row, remember row nine, and derive row seven from it under pressure. That is the difference between carrying twelve facts and carrying a structure.
तीसरा टुकड़ा। ये तीन rows outcome बताती हैं — daughter cells असल में क्या लेकर जाते हैं। और उनमें से आख़िरी पूरे chapter की सबसे ज़्यादा पूछी जाने वाली line है।
तीन rows. Daughters का chromosome number, उनका genetic make up, और key anaphase में क्या separate होता है।
Daughters का chromosome number. Mitosis, parent जैसा — two n से two n. Meiosis, parent का आधा — two n से n. यही equational बनाम reductional वाला फ़र्क़ है, label की जगह outcome की शक्ल में।

Daughters का genetic make up. Mitosis, parent के समान। Meiosis, genetically distinct — varied. और ग़ौर कीजिए ये दो अलग दावे हैं। Mitosis parent से number और content, दोनों में मेल खाता है; meiosis दोनों में अलग है।

Key anaphase में क्या separate होता है। Mitosis, sister chromatids. Meiosis — और ये दो हिस्सों वाला जवाब है — anaphase one में homologues, anaphase two में sister chromatids. दोनों हिस्से दीजिए। जो जवाब सिर्फ़ homologues कहे वो आधा ही सही है।
ये row पूरे chapter की सबसे ज़्यादा पूछी जाने वाली line है। हमने इसे हर part में flag किया, और ये रही आख़िरी बार। अगर revision का time कम है, तो यही वो row है जो पक्की होनी चाहिए।

और causal link देखिए, क्योंकि इसका मतलब है आपको इनमें से एक ही row चाहिए। Row nine, row seven की वजह है। एक जोड़ी को अलग करने से count आधा होता है। एक chromosome के अपने chromatids को अलग करने से नहीं। तो क्या separate होता है, वही तय करता है कि daughters को क्या मिलेगा।
तो अगर आपको सिर्फ़ एक row याद रह सकती है, तो row nine याद रखिए, और दबाव में उससे row seven derive कीजिए। बारह facts उठाने और एक structure उठाने में यही फ़र्क़ है।

board_events.text: Reductional or equational — MITOSIS: equational. MEIOSIS: Meiosis I reductional, Meiosis II equational.
Where it occurs — MITOSIS: throughout the body; plant meristems. MEIOSIS: germ-line / meiocytes only.
Function — MITOSIS: growth, repair, replacement. MEIOSIS: gamete/spore formation; variation.
A useful one-line summary: MITOSIS COPIES. MEIOSIS HALVES-AND-SHUFFLES.
Copies $\Rightarrow$ identical, same number, no pairing, no crossing over. Halves-and-shuffles $\Rightarrow$ n, varied, synapsis, recombination.
In a 'differentiate' answer, always write it as a TABLE with a Feature column — not as prose.

segments.text: Final bite of the table. Three rows, and then the sentence that compresses all twelve.
Reductional or equational, where it occurs, and function. Then the black bar at the bottom.

Reductional or equational. Mitosis, equational. Meiosis — again a two part answer — Meiosis one reductional, Meiosis two equational. Never write meiosis is reductional as a flat statement. Half of it is not.
Where it occurs. Mitosis, throughout the body and in plant meristems. Meiosis, germ line and meiocytes only. That is the life cycle context from the first half of this part, now sitting in the table.
Function. Mitosis, growth, repair, replacement. Meiosis, gamete and spore formation, and variation. Note that meiosis gets two functions — making the cells, and varying them. Both are worth naming.
And here is the one line summary for all twelve rows. Mitosis copies. Meiosis halves and shuffles. Six words, and almost every row can be regenerated from them.

Test it. Copies implies identical daughters, same number, no pairing, no crossing over — that is four rows. Halves and shuffles implies n, varied, synapsis, recombination — that is four more. The summary is not a slogan; it is a compression.

One presentation point for the Boards. In a differentiate answer, always write it as a table with a feature column. Not as prose. Examiners award a mark per correct row, and a table makes each row unmissable — a paragraph buries them.
Table का आख़िरी टुकड़ा। तीन rows, और फिर वो वाक्य जो बारहों को समेट देता है।
Reductional या equational, कहाँ होता है, और function. फिर सबसे नीचे काली पट्टी।

Reductional या equational. Mitosis, equational. Meiosis — फिर दो हिस्सों वाला जवाब — Meiosis one reductional, Meiosis two equational. Meiosis is reductional को सपाट बयान की तरह कभी मत लिखिए। उसका आधा हिस्सा नहीं है।
कहाँ होता है। Mitosis, पूरे शरीर में और plant meristems में। Meiosis, सिर्फ़ germ line और meiocytes में। यही इस part के पहले आधे हिस्से का life cycle context है, अब table में बैठा हुआ।

Function. Mitosis, growth, repair, replacement. Meiosis, gamete और spore formation, और variation. ग़ौर कीजिए meiosis को दो functions मिलते हैं — cells बनाना, और उन्हें varied करना। दोनों का नाम लेना बनता है।
और ये रहा बारहों rows का एक line वाला सार। Mitosis copies. Meiosis halves and shuffles. छह शब्द, और लगभग हर row इन्हीं से दोबारा बनाई जा सकती है।

इसे जाँचिए। Copies का मतलब identical daughters, same number, कोई pairing नहीं, कोई crossing over नहीं — ये चार rows हो गईं। Halves and shuffles का मतलब n, varied, synapsis, recombination — ये चार और। ये सार कोई नारा नहीं; ये एक compression है।

Boards के लिए एक presentation point. Differentiate वाले जवाब में हमेशा एक table लिखिए, feature column के साथ। Prose में नहीं। Examiners हर सही row पर एक mark देते हैं, और table हर row को साफ़ दिखा देती है — paragraph उन्हें दबा देता है।

board_events.text: 1. CHROMOSOME NUMBER — count the CENTROMERES. Written 2n or n.
2. CHROMATIDS PER CHROMOSOME — always just 1 or 2.
3. DNA AMOUNT — in 'C' units. Baseline: an unreplicated diploid cell holds 2C.
The whole numerical difficulty of this chapter is that these three do NOT move together.
So set up three columns. Never hold them in your head.
Take a diploid cell with chromosome number 2n and a baseline DNA amount of 2C, and let us walk it.

segments.text: Now the numerical skill. The most tested numerical skill in this chapter is tracking three quantities through every stage — and the errors all come from collapsing them into fewer than three.
Three panels for three quantities. Chromosome number. Chromatids per chromosome. And D N A amount, in C units.
Quantity one, chromosome number. And the operational rule, which has served us since part one — count the centromeres, not the rods. Written as two n or n.

Quantity two, chromatids per chromosome. And this one is easy, because it only ever takes two values. One, or two. Never three, never four. If your working produces anything else, you have made an error.

Quantity three, D N A amount, measured in C units. And you must fix the baseline before anything else. An unreplicated diploid cell holds two C. That is the reference point every other value is measured against.

And here is the whole numerical difficulty of this chapter, stated once. These three quantities do not move together. S phase moves one of them. Meiosis one moves a different one. Meiosis two moves a third combination. They are on three separate schedules.

So the discipline is mechanical. Set up three columns on the page. Never hold them in your head, because the moment you do, one will drag the others along and you will halve something that did not halve.
So let us take a diploid cell with chromosome number two n and a baseline D N A amount of two C, and walk it through both routes. First the mitotic route, then the meiotic route.
अब numerical skill. इस chapter की सबसे ज़्यादा जाँची जाने वाली numerical skill है हर stage में तीन quantities को track करना — और सारी ग़लतियाँ इन्हें तीन से कम में मिला देने से आती हैं।
तीन quantities के लिए तीन panels. Chromosome number. हर chromosome में chromatids. और D N A amount, C units में।
पहली quantity, chromosome number. और operational नियम, जो part one से हमारे काम आ रहा है — rods मत गिनिए, centromeres गिनिए। Two n या n लिखा जाता है।
दूसरी quantity, हर chromosome में chromatids. और ये आसान है, क्योंकि इसकी सिर्फ़ दो values होती हैं। एक, या दो। कभी तीन नहीं, कभी चार नहीं। अगर आपकी working कुछ और दे, तो ग़लती हो गई है।
तीसरी quantity, D N A amount, C units में। और सबसे पहले baseline तय करनी होगी। एक unreplicated diploid cell में two C होता है। यही वो reference point है जिससे बाक़ी हर value नापी जाती है।

और यहाँ इस chapter की पूरी numerical मुश्किल, एक बार में। ये तीनों quantities साथ नहीं चलतीं। S phase एक को हिलाता है। Meiosis one दूसरी को। Meiosis two तीसरा combination हिलाता है। ये तीन अलग schedules पर हैं।
तो discipline mechanical है। काग़ज़ पर तीन columns बना लीजिए। इन्हें दिमाग़ में कभी मत रखिए, क्योंकि जिस पल आप रखेंगे, एक दूसरों को खींच ले जाएगी और आप कुछ ऐसा आधा कर देंगे जो आधा हुआ ही नहीं।
तो एक diploid cell लेते हैं जिसका chromosome number two n है और baseline D N A amount two C, और उसे दोनों रास्तों से चलाते हैं। पहले mitotic रास्ता, फिर meiotic.

board_events.text: G1 (before S): chromosome number 2n, chromatids 1, DNA 2C.
After S / G2: chromosome number 2n (UNCHANGED), chromatids 2, DNA 4C.
After mitosis (each daughter): chromosome number 2n, chromatids 1, DNA 2C.
Row 3 is IDENTICAL to row 1. Mitosis returns the cell exactly to where it started.
That round trip IS what 'copies' means. The cell goes 2C, 4C, 2C and ends where it began.
And it shows why S phase must come BEFORE the division, not after.

segments.text: Take the mitotic route first, because it is the shorter one and it sets the pattern.
Three rows. G one before S. Then after S, which is the same as G two. Then after mitosis. Read down each column and watch what moves.
G one, before S phase. Chromosome number two n. Chromatids per chromosome, one. D N A, two C. That is our starting state, and note the D N A is at its baseline.

After S phase, which is the same as G two. Chromosome number, still two n — unchanged. Chromatids, now two. D N A, now four C. So S phase moved two of the three columns, and left the chromosome number completely alone.
After mitosis, in each daughter. Chromosome number two n. Chromatids, back to one. D N A, back to two C.
And now look at what that means. Row three is identical to row one. Two n, one, two C — the same three numbers we started with. Mitosis returns the cell exactly to where it started.

That round trip is what copies means, made numerical. The cell goes two C, four C, two C, and ends where it began — except now there are two of it. Double, then halve, and you are back to where you were.

And the table shows why S phase must come before the division rather than after. The doubling in row two is what row three spends. If you divided without doubling first, each daughter would get one C, and the lineage would run down to nothing.
पहले mitotic रास्ता लीजिए, क्योंकि वो छोटा है और वही pattern बना देता है।
तीन rows. S से पहले G one. फिर S के बाद, जो G two जैसा ही है। फिर mitosis के बाद। हर column में नीचे पढ़िए और देखिए क्या हिलता है।
G one, S phase से पहले। Chromosome number two n. हर chromosome में chromatids, एक। D N A, two C. यही हमारी शुरुआती हालत है, और ग़ौर कीजिए D N A अपनी baseline पर है।
S phase के बाद, जो G two जैसा है। Chromosome number, अब भी two n — unchanged. Chromatids, अब दो। D N A, अब four C. तो S phase ने तीन में से दो columns हिलाए, और chromosome number को बिल्कुल नहीं छुआ।
Mitosis के बाद, हर daughter में। Chromosome number two n. Chromatids, वापस एक। D N A, वापस two C.
और अब देखिए इसका मतलब क्या है। Row तीन, row एक के समान है। Two n, एक, two C — वही तीन numbers जिनसे हमने शुरू किया था। Mitosis cell को ठीक वहीं लौटा देता है जहाँ से वो चला था।

वही round trip है जिसे copies कहते हैं, numbers में। Cell two C, four C, two C से गुज़रता है, और वहीं ख़त्म होता है जहाँ से शुरू किया — फ़र्क़ बस ये कि अब वो दो हैं। Double कीजिए, फिर आधा, और आप वहीं हैं जहाँ थे।

और table दिखाती है कि S phase division से पहले क्यों आना चाहिए, बाद में क्यों नहीं। Row दो की doubling वही है जो row तीन ख़र्च करती है। अगर आप पहले double किए बिना divide करते, तो हर daughter को one C मिलता, और वंश घटते-घटते ख़त्म हो जाता।

board_events.text: Meiocyte in G2 (before Meiosis I): chromosome number 2n, chromatids 2, DNA 4C.
After Meiosis I (each cell): chromosome number n (HALVED), chromatids 2 (unchanged), DNA 2C.
After Meiosis II (each of 4 cells): chromosome number n (unchanged), chromatids 1 (HALVED), DNA 1C.
Each division halves exactly ONE of the first two columns — never both.
But the DNA column halves at BOTH. That is why the gamete ends at 1C, a quarter of the G2 value.
Compare the two tables: mitosis ends where it started. Meiosis ends at half the number and half the DNA.

segments.text: Now the meiotic route. Same three columns, same starting D N A, and a completely different destination.
Three rows again. The meiocyte in G two. After Meiosis one. After Meiosis two. Read down the columns and watch which one halves where.

The meiocyte in G two, before Meiosis one. Chromosome number two n. Chromatids, two. D N A, four C. And notice this row is identical to the after S row of the mitotic table — the same pre meiotic S phase did the same job.

After Meiosis one, in each cell. Chromosome number, n — halved. Chromatids, still two — unchanged. D N A, two C. So Meiosis one halved the number and the D N A, and left the chromatids completely alone.

After Meiosis two, in each of the four cells. Chromosome number, still n — unchanged. Chromatids, now one — halved. D N A, one C. Meiosis two halved the chromatids and the D N A, and left the number alone.

So read the pattern, because it is beautifully regular. Each division halves exactly one of the first two columns, never both. Meiosis one takes the number. Meiosis two takes the chromatids. They divide the labour precisely.

But the D N A column halves at both divisions. Four C, two C, one C. That is why the gamete ends at one C — a quarter of the four C we started from. The D N A is the only quantity that gets reduced twice.

So compare the two tables and the whole chapter is in the contrast. Mitosis ends exactly where it started. Meiosis ends at half the number and half the D N A of the diploid parent. Same starting cell, same S phase, two destinations.
अब meiotic रास्ता। वही तीन columns, वही शुरुआती D N A, और एक बिल्कुल अलग मंज़िल।
फिर तीन rows. G two में meiocyte. Meiosis one के बाद। Meiosis two के बाद। Columns में नीचे पढ़िए और देखिए कौन सी कहाँ आधी होती है।
G two में meiocyte, Meiosis one से पहले। Chromosome number two n. Chromatids, दो। D N A, four C. और ग़ौर कीजिए ये row, mitotic table की after S row जैसी है — वही pre meiotic S phase ने वही काम किया।
Meiosis one के बाद, हर cell में। Chromosome number, n — आधा। Chromatids, अब भी दो — unchanged. D N A, two C. तो Meiosis one ने number और D N A आधे किए, और chromatids को बिल्कुल नहीं छुआ।
Meiosis two के बाद, चारों cells में से हर एक में। Chromosome number, अब भी n — unchanged. Chromatids, अब एक — आधे। D N A, one C. Meiosis two ने chromatids और D N A आधे किए, और number को नहीं छुआ।

तो pattern पढ़िए, क्योंकि वो बेहद नियमित है। हर division पहले दो columns में से ठीक एक को आधा करता है, कभी दोनों को नहीं। Meiosis one number लेता है। Meiosis two chromatids लेता है। वो काम बिल्कुल ठीक बाँट लेते हैं।
पर D N A column दोनों divisions पर आधी होती है। Four C, two C, one C. इसीलिए gamete one C पर ख़त्म होता है — उस four C का एक चौथाई जहाँ से हमने शुरू किया। D N A अकेली quantity है जो दो बार घटती है।

तो दोनों tables मिलाइए और पूरा chapter उसी contrast में है। Mitosis ठीक वहीं ख़त्म होता है जहाँ से शुरू हुआ। Meiosis diploid parent के आधे number और आधी D N A पर ख़त्म होता है। वही शुरुआती cell, वही S phase, दो मंज़िलें।
